q: Which of the following is one of the fundamental principles of British life?
o: Rule by a single political party
e: The fundamental principles are democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of different faiths and beliefs, and participation in community life.

q: Which countries make up Great Britain?
o: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
e: Great Britain is England, Scotland and Wales. The UK also includes Northern Ireland.

q: In which year did the Romans, led by Emperor Claudius, successfully invade Britain?
e: Julius Caesar's invasion in 55 BC failed; Claudius invaded successfully in AD 43.

q: At which battle in 1066 did William, Duke of Normandy, defeat the English king Harold?
e: The Norman Conquest began with the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

q: Which charter of 1215 limited the power of the king for the first time?
e: King John was forced to agree to the Magna Carta in 1215.

q: Which king broke away from the Roman Catholic Church and established the Church of England?
e: Henry VIII broke from Rome when the Pope refused to allow his divorce.

q: In which year was the Spanish Armada defeated?
e: The Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588 during the reign of Elizabeth I.

q: Who is generally regarded as the first Prime Minister of Great Britain?
e: Sir Robert Walpole was Prime Minister from 1721 to 1742.

q: Who commanded the British fleet at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
e: Nelson was killed at Trafalgar; Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square commemorates him.

q: Who is regarded as the founder of modern nursing?
e: Florence Nightingale nursed soldiers in the Crimean War and founded a nurse training school at St Thomas' Hospital in 1860.

q: When did the First World War end?
e: The war ended at 11.00 am on 11 November 1918 with Britain and its allies victorious.

q: On which date is St David's Day, the patron saint's day of Wales?
e: St David's Day is 1 March; St Patrick's is 17 March, St George's 23 April, St Andrew's 30 November.

q: Which tennis tournament is the oldest in the world?
e: The Wimbledon Championships are the oldest tennis tournament in the world.

q: Who wrote the novel 'Pride and Prejudice'?
e: Jane Austen's novels include Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility.

q: Which composer wrote the 'Pomp and Circumstance Marches'?
e: Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1 is played at the Last Night of the Proms.

q: In which part of the UK is the Giant's Causeway?
e: The Giant's Causeway on the north-east coast of Northern Ireland is made of thousands of hexagonal columns.

q: What is 'Big Ben'?
o: The nickname for the great bell of the clock at the Houses of Parliament
The official name of the Houses of Parliament
A famous bridge over the River Thames
The largest bell in St Paul's Cathedral
e: The clock tower itself was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

q: Haggis is a traditional food from which country?
e: Haggis is a sheep's stomach stuffed with offal, suet, onions and oatmeal.

q: How many Members of Parliament (MPs) sit in the House of Commons?
e: There are 650 parliamentary constituencies, each electing one MP.

q: Where is the official London residence of the Prime Minister?
e: The Prime Minister lives at 10 Downing Street and also has a country house, Chequers.

q: How many members of the public sit on a jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
e: Jury trials are held in the Crown Court for serious criminal cases.

q: Which telephone numbers can you call in an emergency to reach the police, fire service or ambulance?
e: Use 999 or 112 only in a genuine emergency.

q: What kind of system of government does the UK have?
o: A parliamentary democracy with a constitutional monarch
e: The monarch is head of state but the elected Parliament makes the laws.

q: Which government minister is responsible for the economy?
e: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy.

q: Which of these is a responsibility shared by everyone who lives in the UK?
o: To respect and obey the law
To vote for the party in government
To attend a religious service each week
e: Responsibilities include respecting and obeying the law, respecting the rights of others and treating others fairly.

q: What is the status of the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man?
o: They are Crown dependencies with their own governments
They are part of the United Kingdom
e: They are closely linked with the UK but are not part of it.

q: When did the Roman army leave Britain?
e: The Romans left in AD 410 to defend other parts of their empire.

q: What did the Romans build in the north of England to keep out tribes from what is now Scotland?
e: Parts of Hadrian's Wall, including forts such as Housesteads, can still be seen today.

q: Which Stone Age village on Orkney is the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe?
e: Skara Brae shows how people lived near the end of the Stone Age.

q: Which Anglo-Saxon king united kingdoms in England and defeated the Vikings?
e: Alfred the Great united the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and defeated the Vikings.

q: What was the Domesday Book?
o: A book of prayers for the Church of England
A record of towns, villages, people and animals in England made by William the Conqueror
A list of laws written by King John
A history of the Roman invasion
e: It gives a picture of society in England just after the Norman Conquest.

q: At which battle in 1314 did Robert the Bruce defeat the English?
e: Victory at Bannockburn kept Scotland unconquered by the English.

q: What was the Black Death that arrived in Britain in 1348?
o: A great fire that destroyed London
A famine caused by a failed potato harvest
A Viking army that attacked the east coast
A disease, probably a form of plague, that killed around one third of England's population
e: Labour shortages after the Black Death led to new social classes and higher wages.

q: Which wars ended with the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485?
e: Henry Tudor (Henry VII) defeated Richard III and became king.

q: Which Act of 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain?
e: The Act of Union joined England (with Wales) and Scotland under one Parliament.

q: When is St Andrew's Day, the patron saint's day of Scotland?
e: St Andrew's Day is an official holiday in Scotland.

q: Who is the spiritual leader of the Church of England?
o: The Speaker of the House of Commons
The Moderator of the General Assembly
e: The monarch is Supreme Governor; the Archbishop of Canterbury is the spiritual leader.

q: Where are the BBC Proms concerts mainly held?
e: The Proms is an eight-week summer season of orchestral music organised by the BBC since 1927.

q: In 1954, who became the first man to run a mile in under four minutes?
e: Bannister ran the first sub-four-minute mile in 1954.

q: Which famous novel was written by Charles Dickens?
e: Dickens also wrote Great Expectations. Treasure Island is by Robert Louis Stevenson.

q: On which date is Boxing Day?
e: Boxing Day, the day after Christmas Day, is a public holiday.

q: In which part of the UK is the Eden Project, with its huge greenhouses housing plants from around the world?
e: The Eden Project is an educational charity in Cornwall.

q: Who is the Supreme Governor of the Church of England?
e: The monarch is not allowed to marry anyone who is not Protestant.

q: Who keeps order during political debates in the House of Commons?
e: The Speaker is an MP chosen by other MPs and is politically neutral.

q: Where does the Scottish Parliament sit?
e: The Scottish Parliament was formed in 1999 and sits at Holyrood.

q: Which court is the final court of appeal for all civil cases in the UK?
e: The Supreme Court is the highest court of appeal in the UK.

q: How often does Prime Minister's Questions take place?
o: Once a year at the State Opening
Every week while Parliament is sitting
e: Members of the House of Commons question the Prime Minister weekly.

q: What is the job of the party 'whips' in Parliament?
o: To count the votes at a general election
To ensure discipline and attendance of MPs at votes
To chair debates in the House of Commons
To advise the monarch on new laws
e: Whips make sure their party's MPs attend and vote.

q: Which of these is a fundamental freedom in the UK?
o: Freedom to ignore laws you disagree with
e: UK freedoms include belief and religion, speech, freedom from unfair discrimination and the right to a fair trial.

q: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
e: The UK capitals are London, Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.

q: In which English county is Stonehenge?
e: Stonehenge was probably a special gathering place for seasonal ceremonies.

q: Where was an Anglo-Saxon king buried with his ship and treasure?
e: The burial site was discovered at Sutton Hoo in 1939.

q: What does the Bayeux Tapestry show?
o: The Norman invasion and the Battle of Hastings
The defeat of the Spanish Armada
e: The tapestry can still be seen in France.

q: In 1415, which king won the Battle of Agincourt against France?
e: Agincourt was one of the most famous battles of the Hundred Years War.

q: Who wrote 'The Canterbury Tales'?
e: The Canterbury Tales are stories of pilgrims travelling to Canterbury.

q: Which of Henry VIII's wives was the mother of Elizabeth I and was executed?
e: Anne Boleyn was executed at the Tower of London.

q: What happened in London in 1666?
e: The fire destroyed much of the city, including the old St Paul's Cathedral.

q: Which crosses make up the Union Flag?
o: The crosses of St George, St Andrew and St David
The crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick
The crosses of St George and St Andrew only
The crosses of St George, St David and St Patrick
e: Wales is not represented on the Union Flag because it was already united with England.

q: What happened on 6 June 1944 (D-Day)?
o: British troops were evacuated from Dunkirk
The Second World War ended in Europe
e: The D-Day landings began the liberation of Western Europe.

q: On which date is Remembrance Day?
e: People wear poppies and hold a two-minute silence at 11.00 am.

q: What kind of church is the Church of Scotland?
e: It is governed by ministers and elders; its chairperson is the Moderator.

q: Which play did William Shakespeare write?
e: Shakespeare also wrote Hamlet, Macbeth and A Midsummer Night's Dream.

q: Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean won Olympic gold in 1984 in which sport?
e: They won gold at the 1984 Winter Olympics.

q: The Turner Prize is awarded in which field?
e: The Turner Prize was established in 1984 and is named after J. M. W. Turner.

q: On which date is Halloween?
e: Halloween has ancient origins; children often go 'trick or treating'.

q: What is Loch Lomond?
o: The largest expanse of fresh water in mainland Britain
e: Loch Lomond is part of the Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park.

q: What is the role of the Leader of the Opposition?
o: To lead the House of Lords
To chair debates in the House of Commons
To lead the second-largest party, which is not in government
e: The Leader of the Opposition appoints a shadow cabinet.

q: Which voting system is used to elect MPs to the House of Commons?
e: The candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins.

q: Who sits in the House of Lords?
o: Life peers, hereditary peers and Church of England bishops
MPs who have retired from the Commons
e: Members of the House of Lords are not elected by the people.

q: What is Hansard?
o: The official report of everything said in Parliament
A newspaper owned by the government
A list of people registered to vote
e: Hansard is available to the public.

q: Which of these is true about most magistrates in England and Wales?
o: They are paid judges with legal qualifications
They are usually unpaid and do not need legal qualifications
They are elected by the public
e: Magistrates (Justices of the Peace) are volunteers who receive training.

q: What does the Council of Europe do?
o: Protects and promotes human rights, democracy and the rule of law
Makes laws that all member states must follow
e: It has no power to make laws but drew up the European Convention on Human Rights.

q: What do new citizens do at a citizenship ceremony?
o: Promise to vote at every election
Swear loyalty to the Prime Minister
Make an oath or affirmation of allegiance and a pledge
e: New citizens swear or affirm loyalty to the monarch and pledge to respect UK laws and values.

q: Which of these is a British overseas territory?
e: Other overseas territories include St Helena; the Isle of Man and Channel Islands are Crown dependencies.

q: Around how long ago did Britain become separated from the continent by the Channel?
e: Before that, early people could walk across a land bridge.

q: Which Dutch prince was invited to invade England in 1688 and became King William III?
e: The 1688 change of monarch is known as the 'Glorious Revolution'.

q: Which missionary founded a monastery on the island of Iona?
e: St Columba brought Christianity to the north from Iona, off the west coast of Scotland.

q: Where did the Vikings who invaded Britain from AD 789 come from?
e: Vikings raided coastal towns and later settled in parts of Britain.

q: Who united the people of the north under one ruler, partly as a defence against the Vikings?
e: The kingdom became known as Scotland.

q: Which king annexed Wales to England with the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284?
e: Edward I built castles such as Conwy and Caernarvon.

q: What does the Tudor rose represent?
o: The joining of the houses of York and Lancaster
The union of England and Scotland
e: Henry VII married Elizabeth of York, uniting the red and white roses.

q: Who sailed around the world in his ship, the Golden Hind?
e: Drake was one of the commanders against the Spanish Armada.

q: Who took the title of 'Lord Protector' after the execution of Charles I?
e: England was a republic, known as the Commonwealth, under Cromwell.

q: In which country is Snowdonia (Eryri)?
e: Snowdonia is a national park in north Wales; Snowdon is the highest mountain in Wales.

q: When is Mothering Sunday?
o: The Sunday three weeks before Easter
e: Children send cards or buy gifts for their mothers.

q: Which famous work was written by Gustav Holst?
e: The Planets is a suite of seven pieces, each representing a planet.

q: What is Dame Ellen MacArthur famous for?
o: The first solo climb of Everest by a British woman
The fastest solo sailing journey around the world
The first woman to win Wimbledon
Five Olympic gold medals in rowing
e: She became the fastest person to sail around the world single-handed.

q: Which famous detective was created by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle?
e: Conan Doyle was a Scottish doctor and writer.

q: Which parts of the UK have banks that issue their own banknotes?
e: Scottish and Northern Irish banknotes are valid currency across the UK.

q: Royal Ascot is a famous event in which sport?
e: Royal Ascot is a five-day race meeting in Berkshire attended by the royal family.

q: How often must a general election be held?
e: MPs are elected at a general election held at least every five years.

q: Which minister is responsible for crime, policing and immigration?
e: The Home Secretary leads the Home Office.

q: What is Chequers?
e: The Prime Minister's official London home is 10 Downing Street.

q: When is a by-election held?
o: When a new monarch is crowned
When an MP dies or resigns
e: A by-election chooses a new MP for that constituency.

q: What is NATO?
o: A group of European and North American countries that have agreed to help each other if they come under attack
A group of countries that were part of the British Empire
A trade union for British workers
An organisation that sets the price of oil
e: NATO also aims to maintain peace between its members.

q: Which law protects people from discrimination in Great Britain?
e: It protects people on grounds such as age, disability, sex, race and religion.

q: Which language, besides English, is widely spoken in Wales?
e: Welsh is taught in schools and appears on official signs in Wales.

q: What is the capital city of Scotland?
e: Edinburgh is the home of the Scottish Parliament.

q: Around when did the Bronze Age begin in Britain?
e: People learned to make bronze and were buried in round barrows.

q: What happened when Julius Caesar led an invasion of Britain in 55 BC?
o: He conquered the whole of Britain
e: Britain was not invaded successfully until AD 43.

q: Who was sent to bring Christianity to the south of England and became the first Archbishop of Canterbury?
e: St Augustine arrived in AD 597.

q: What was the Danelaw?
o: An area of England where the Vikings settled and ruled
A Roman road between London and York
e: Many place names in the north and east of England come from Viking languages.

q: Which of Henry VIII's wives gave birth to his son, Edward VI?
e: Jane Seymour died shortly after Edward was born.

q: Which document of 1689 confirmed the rights of Parliament and limited the power of the monarch?
e: It also confirmed that the monarch must be a Protestant.

q: Who led the women's suffrage movement and founded the Women's Social and Political Union?
e: Her supporters, the suffragettes, campaigned for women to have the vote.

q: At which battle in 1815 did the Duke of Wellington defeat Napoleon?
e: The battle ended the Napoleonic Wars.

q: What happened at Dunkirk in 1940?
o: British troops were rescued from France by many small boats
The RAF defeated the German air force
e: The 'Dunkirk spirit' describes courage in the face of difficulty.

q: When is St Patrick's Day, the patron saint's day of Northern Ireland?
e: St Patrick's Day is an official holiday in Northern Ireland.

q: What is Hogmanay?
o: New Year's Eve, as celebrated in Scotland
e: New Year's Day (1 January) is a public holiday across the UK, and 2 January is also one in Scotland.

q: What is remembered on Bonfire Night, 5 November?
o: The end of the Second World War
The failed plot to blow up Parliament in 1605
The defeat of the Spanish Armada
e: Guy Fawkes and others tried to kill the Protestant king with gunpowder.

q: Who wrote the music for 'Jesus Christ Superstar', 'Cats' and 'The Phantom of the Opera'?
e: Lloyd Webber's musicals have been popular across the world.

q: In which sport did Sir Chris Hoy win six Olympic gold medals?
e: Sir Chris Hoy is a Scottish cyclist.

q: Which town in Scotland is known as the home of golf?
e: The modern game of golf traces back to 15th- century Scotland.

q: Which country is the 'Ulster fry' traditionally associated with?
e: An Ulster fry is a fried breakfast that includes soda bread and potato bread.

q: Who appoints the senior ministers who form the Cabinet?
e: The Cabinet usually has around 20 senior MPs.

q: Which court deals with most minor criminal cases in England and Wales?
e: In Scotland, minor cases go to a Justice of the Peace Court.

q: At what times are polling stations open on election day?
e: You can also vote by post if you register for a postal vote.

q: What is the Commonwealth?
o: A voluntary association of countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire
A military alliance of European countries
A group of countries that share one government
The name for the UK, Isle of Man and Channel Islands
e: The monarch is head of the Commonwealth; it has no power over its members.

q: Which organisation collects taxes in the UK?
e: Income tax is usually deducted from wages through the PAYE system.

q: Where does the Northern Ireland Assembly meet?
e: The Assembly was created after the 1998 Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement.

q: Which of these is a responsibility you share with others living in the UK?
o: To ignore laws you disagree with
To look after the area in which you live and the environment
To help only people from your own background
To avoid speaking to your neighbours
e: Looking after your area and the environment is a shared responsibility.

q: What is the national flag of the United Kingdom called?
o: The Union Flag (often called the Union Jack)
e: It combines the crosses of England, Scotland and Ireland.

q: When were the first farmers believed to have arrived in Britain?
e: Farming changed how people lived in Britain.

q: For about how long did the Romans stay in Britain?
e: They stayed from AD 43 until AD 410.

q: After the Romans left, which tribes invaded Britain from northern Europe?
e: Their languages formed the basis of modern- day English.

q: What system of land ownership did the Normans use?
e: The king gave land to lords in return for help in war.

q: What was the Reformation?
o: The return of the monarchy in 1660
The growth of factories in the 19th century
A movement against the authority of the Pope and the Roman Catholic Church
The rebuilding of London after the Great Fire
e: It led to the creation of Protestant churches.

q: Which Tudor monarch introduced the Book of Common Prayer?
e: Edward VI was strongly Protestant; a version of the prayer book is still used.

q: In which year did the English Civil War begin?
e: The war was between Charles I's supporters and Parliament.

q: Which famous scientist, a member of the Royal Society, showed how gravity applies to the whole universe?
e: Newton's most famous work was Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica.

q: Which famous cathedral did Sir Christopher Wren design after the Great Fire of London?
e: Wren rebuilt many London churches after 1666.

q: What animal appears on the national flag of Wales?
e: Wales is not represented on the Union Flag.

q: What does Easter commemorate?
o: The start of the new year
The death of Jesus Christ on Good Friday and his rising from the dead on Easter Sunday
e: Good Friday and Easter Monday are public holidays in many parts of the UK.

q: On which date is Valentine's Day?
e: Lovers and partners exchange cards and gifts.

q: Henry Moore is famous for which kind of art?
e: Henry Moore is best known for his bronze and stone sculptures.

q: At the 2012 Olympic Games, Mo Farah won gold medals in which events?
e: He was the first Briton to win the Olympic 10,000 metres gold.

q: Which famous horse race is held at Aintree, near Liverpool?
e: The Grand National is a famous steeplechase.

q: When are pantomimes traditionally performed?
e: Pantomimes are light-hearted plays based on fairy stories.

q: What does the monarch's speech at the State Opening of Parliament set out?
o: The government's policies for the next parliamentary session
The tax rates for the next ten years
The results of the general election
e: The speech is written for the monarch by the government.

q: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, which court hears serious criminal cases with a judge and jury?
e: In Scotland, serious cases are heard in a Sheriff Court or the High Court.

q: How often is the electoral register updated?
o: Every ten years with the census
e: You must be on the register to vote.

q: How are local council services mainly funded?
o: By money from central government and by council tax
e: Council tax is paid by residents of each local authority.

q: The UK is a permanent member of the Security Council of which organisation?
e: The UN was set up after the Second World War to prevent war and promote peace.

q: Which court deals with young people accused of crimes, aged 10 to 17, in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
e: The young person's name cannot be published in the press.

q: Which of these is one of the fundamental principles of British life?
o: Obedience to a single political party
Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs
e: Tolerance of different faiths and beliefs is a core British value.

q: Which country in the UK has the largest population?
e: About 84% of the UK population lives in England.

q: Which of these did the Romans do in Britain?
o: Built roads and public buildings and created a structure of law
e: The Romans also introduced new plants and animals.

q: Who was the first woman Prime Minister of the UK?
e: Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990.

q: Which Scottish inventor's work on steam power helped the Industrial Revolution?
e: Watt improved the steam engine in the 18th century.

q: What is Richard Arkwright known for?
o: Developing horse-driven spinning mills that used one machine
e: He made factory production more efficient and profitable.

q: What did the Bessemer process allow?
o: The mass production of cotton cloth
e: It helped Britain's shipbuilding and railway industries grow.

q: In which year did Queen Victoria become queen, aged 18?
e: Victoria reigned until 1901, almost 64 years.

q: What did the Emancipation Act of 1833 do?
o: Gave women the right to vote
Abolished slavery throughout the British Empire
e: The slave trade itself had been abolished in 1807.

q: What did the Reform Act of 1832 do?
o: Greatly increased the number of people with the right to vote
Gave all women the right to vote
e: It also abolished old 'pocket' and 'rotten' boroughs.

q: What caused the Irish famine of the mid-1840s?
o: The failure of the potato crop
e: Over a million people died and many emigrated.

q: In which year did the Battle of the Somme take place, with around 60,000 British casualties on the first day?
e: The battle began on 1 July 1916.

q: What is Diwali?
o: A Jewish festival lasting eight days
A festival of lights celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs
The end of Ramadan for Muslims
e: A famous celebration takes place in Leicester.

q: What is the Eisteddfod?
o: A Welsh festival of music, poetry and dance
A horse race in Northern Ireland
e: The National Eisteddfod of Wales is one of the largest such festivals in Europe.

q: Which pair wrote comic operas such as 'HMS Pinafore' and 'The Mikado'?
e: Their light operas often made fun of popular culture and politics.

q: Which poet wrote about his experiences in the First World War, including 'Anthem for Doomed Youth'?
e: Wilfred Owen was killed in 1918, a week before the war ended.

q: In 2013, Andy Murray became the first British man to win which tournament since 1936?
e: He had won the US Open in 2012, his first Grand Slam singles title.

q: Who guard the Tower of London?
e: The Crown Jewels are kept at the Tower of London.

q: Welsh cakes are a traditional snack from which country?
e: They are made from flour, dried fruit and spices.

q: How many members are there in the Scottish Parliament (MSPs)?
e: They are elected using a form of proportional representation.

q: Which of these is an example of a civil law case?
o: A dispute between a landlord and a tenant
e: Civil law settles disputes between individuals or groups; criminal law covers crimes.

q: If the House of Lords and House of Commons disagree, which can overrule the other?
e: The Lords can suggest amendments, but the Commons has the final say.

q: What does National Insurance pay for?
o: State benefits and services such as the state pension and the NHS
e: Most working people pay National Insurance Contributions.

q: Which of these is a criminal offence in the UK?
o: Forcing someone to marry against their will
Refusing to join a political party
e: Forced marriage is illegal; arranged marriages are legal when both parties agree.

q: To become a permanent resident or citizen, what must you be able to show?
o: That you are married to a British citizen
That you can speak and read English and have a good understanding of life in the UK
That you have a job in the UK
That you own a house in the UK
e: Applicants must pass the Life in the UK test and meet English language requirements.

q: Where does the UK Parliament sit?
e: The Houses of Parliament are at Westminster.

q: Which people did the Romans build Hadrian's Wall to keep out?
e: The Picts were ancestors of the Scottish people.

q: In which year did the Vikings first come to Britain to raid coastal towns?
e: They later stayed and formed communities.

q: By around 1400, which language had become the preferred language of the royal court and Parliament in England?
e: Official documents were also being written in English by then.

q: During the reign of Elizabeth I, where did English settlers begin to colonise?
e: This was the beginning of English colonisation abroad.

q: During the reign of James I, where in Ireland were Protestant settlers given land?
e: This was known as the plantation of Ulster.

q: After his army was defeated, where did Charles II famously hide from Parliament's soldiers?
e: Charles II later returned to the throne at the Restoration in 1660.

q: What is Sake Dean Mahomet known for?
o: Opening the first curry house in Britain and introducing 'shampooing'
e: He opened the Hindoostane Coffee House in London in 1810.

q: Who developed the jet engine in the 1930s?
e: Whittle was a Royal Air Force engineer officer.

q: What was the Battle of Britain in 1940?
o: A naval battle off the coast of France
A battle between Britain and Spain
A battle in the skies in which the RAF defeated the German air force
e: German plans to invade Britain had to be abandoned.

q: When is St George's Day, the patron saint's day of England?
e: St George's Day is not a public holiday.

q: Who painted 'The Hay Wain'?
e: Constable was a landscape painter famous for scenes of Suffolk.

q: At the 2012 London Olympics, Jessica Ennis won gold in which event?
e: The heptathlon includes seven different track and field events.

q: Which countries compete in rugby union's Six Nations Championship?
o: England, Scotland, Wales, Australia, New Zealand and France
England, Wales, Ireland, South Africa, Fiji and Italy
England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy
The four UK countries, Spain and Germany
e: The Six Nations is held every year.

q: Which writer wrote 'Far from the Madding Crowd'?
e: Hardy's novels are often set in rural England.

q: When was the National Trust founded?
e: It cares for historic buildings, coastline and countryside.

q: What does the Sikh festival of Vaisakhi celebrate?
o: The founding of the Sikh community known as the Khalsa
e: Vaisakhi is celebrated on 14 April each year.

q: Who is the head of state of the United Kingdom?
e: The UK is a constitutional monarchy.

q: What do elected Police and Crime Commissioners (PCCs) do?
o: Set local police priorities and the police budget
e: PCCs in England and Wales were first elected in November 2012.

q: Who formally appoints life peers to the House of Lords?
o: The monarch, on the advice of the Prime Minister
The Speaker of the House of Commons
e: Life peers are often people with experience in many fields of life.

q: What is the 'shadow cabinet'?
o: Senior members of the main opposition party who lead the criticism of government ministers
e: The Leader of the Opposition appoints the shadow cabinet.

q: What is the money from TV licences used for?
e: You need a licence to watch or record programmes as they are broadcast.

q: What is the minimum age to drive a car on UK roads?
e: You must have a driving licence and insurance.

q: Which of these is a right protected in the UK?
o: The right to a fair trial
The right to avoid jury service without a reason
The right to break the law in protest
The right to refuse to pay taxes
e: Other rights include freedom of speech and freedom from unfair discrimination.

q: What is the approximate distance from John O'Groats in Scotland to Land's End in England?
e: This is the longest distance on the UK mainland.

q: How did the first people reach Britain during the Stone Age?
o: They walked across a land bridge from Europe
They came by boat from Ireland
e: Britain was still connected to the continent at that time.

q: Who was the Danish king who ruled England in the 11th century?
e: There were English and Danish kings in England in this period.

q: Who was Henry VIII's first wife?
e: Catherine of Aragon was a Spanish princess.

q: Which poet wrote 'Paradise Lost'?
e: Milton also wrote other religious poems in the 17th century.

q: Who were the Huguenots who came to Britain between 1680 and 1720?
e: Many were scientists, bankers, weavers or craftsmen.

q: Which poet wrote 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud' about daffodils?
e: Wordsworth was a leading poet of the Romantic movement.

q: What did laws passed in 1870 and 1882 give married women?
o: The right to keep their own earnings and property
The right to stand for Parliament
The right to a free education
e: Before these laws, a woman's property passed to her husband on marriage.

q: When did the period known as 'the Troubles' begin in Northern Ireland?
e: Over 3,000 people lost their lives in the decades of conflict.

q: In which year was the Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement signed?
e: It led to the establishment of the Northern Ireland Assembly.

q: Which scientists developed IVF (in-vitro fertilisation), with the first 'test-tube baby' born in 1978?
o: Sir Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe
e: The first IVF baby was born in Britain in 1978.

q: What did Sir Steve Redgrave achieve?
o: Gold medals in rowing at five consecutive Olympic Games
Running a mile in under four minutes
e: He is one of Britain's greatest Olympians.

q: Which sport is played in 'The Ashes' series between England and Australia?
e: Cricket matches can last up to five days.

q: What is the Lake District?
o: A group of islands off Wales
A national park in Northern Ireland
e: It is famous for its lakes and mountains; Windermere is in the park.

q: What is Hanukkah?
o: A Jewish festival lasting eight days
A Muslim festival marking the end of Ramadan
e: Candles are lit on a stand with eight candles to remember a struggle for religious freedom.

q: The Man Booker Prize is awarded for what?
o: The best fiction novel of the year
e: It has been awarded since 1968.

q: Where did the Paralympic Games originate?
e: Dr Sir Ludwig Guttmann developed new methods of treatment for spinal injuries there.

q: Which designer and architect from Glasgow is famous for his distinctive style around 1900?
e: He was a major figure in the Arts and Crafts movement in Scotland.

q: Who can vote in UK general elections?
o: Only UK citizens who own property
Only people born in the UK
UK, Irish and qualifying Commonwealth citizens aged 18 or over living in the UK
Anyone living in the UK for more than a year
e: Voters must be on the electoral register.

q: What did the Human Rights Act 1998 do?
o: Incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law
Gave women the right to vote
e: Government and public bodies must follow the rights in the Convention.

q: In England, Scotland and Wales, how old must a car be before it needs an annual MOT test?
e: In Northern Ireland, cars need a test from four years old.

q: What is the legal position of female genital mutilation (FGM) in the UK?
o: It is legal for adults only
It is legal in some parts of the UK
It is legal if a parent agrees
e: Taking a girl abroad for FGM is also a crime.

q: If you cannot get to a polling station on election day, how else can you vote?
o: By writing to the Prime Minister
e: You must register for a postal vote in advance.

q: Which of these is one of the fundamental principles of British life?
e: Taking part in community life, for example by volunteering, is valued.

q: Which part of the UK has a legal system that is different from the rest of the UK?
e: Scotland has its own courts and some different laws.

q: Where are the first farmers in Britain thought to have come from?
e: They built houses, tombs and monuments.

q: At which battle in 1746 was Charles Edward Stuart ('Bonnie Prince Charlie') defeated?
e: He tried to regain the throne for the Stuarts in 1745.

q: Which of Henry VIII's wives was a German princess?
e: Henry VIII married Anne of Cleves for political reasons and divorced her soon after.

q: In which year were women given the right to vote at the age of 21, the same as men?
e: In 1918, women over 30 had been given the vote.

q: In which year did the Second World War end in Europe?
e: Victory in Europe (VE) Day was celebrated on 8 May 1945.

q: Who developed the television in the 1920s?
e: In 1932 Baird made the first television broadcast between London and Glasgow.

q: Which Scottish inventor developed the cash machine (ATM) in the 1960s?
e: Goodfellow also developed the idea of the PIN number.

q: Which party won the general election in 1997, with Tony Blair as Prime Minister?
e: Blair's government introduced devolution to Scotland and Wales.

q: Which parties formed a coalition government in 2010?
o: The Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats
e: David Cameron became Prime Minister.

q: Who wrote the 'Water Music' for King George I?
e: Handel was German-born and became a British citizen.

q: In which city does the 'Fringe' festival take place every summer?
e: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe showcases theatre and comedy.

q: Which sculptor created the 'Angel of the North'?
e: The sculpture stands near Gateshead in north-east England.

q: What do people traditionally eat on Shrove Tuesday?
e: Shrove Tuesday is the day before Lent starts.

q: Who captained the England football team that won the World Cup in 1966?
e: England beat West Germany 4-2 in the 1966 final at Wembley.

q: Which Scottish poet wrote 'Auld Lang Syne', sung at New Year?
e: Burns is often known as 'The Bard' in Scotland.

q: What is 'Capability' Brown famous for?
o: Designing landscaped gardens around country houses
e: His gardens, such as at Blenheim Palace, look natural, with lakes and grassland.

q: Which of these is true about the civil service?
o: Civil servants are elected by the public
Civil servants change after every election
Civil servants must belong to the governing party
e: Civil servants carry out government policy whichever party is in power.

q: Which of these powers stays with the UK Parliament and is not devolved?
e: Immigration, taxation and social security are also mainly UK-wide matters.

q: What is a pressure group?
o: A group of MPs who discipline their party
An organisation that tries to influence government policy
e: Pressure groups are an important part of political life.

q: What is a constituency?
o: A group of MPs from the same party
An area of the country represented by one MP
e: There are 650 constituencies in the UK.

q: If you are asked to do jury service, what must you do?
o: Pay a fee to avoid it
Do it only if you want to
Do it, unless you are not eligible or have a good reason to be excused
e: Anyone on the electoral register may be chosen at random.

q: Who leads the Greater London Authority?
o: The Lord Mayor of the City of London
e: The Mayor of London is elected by Londoners.

q: During which period did Stone Age people first live in Britain?
o: The Stone Age, at least 10,000 years ago
e: The first people lived in Britain during the Stone Age, and for much of that time Britain was connected to the continent by land.

q: The Middle Ages in Britain is the name given to roughly which period?
o: The time from the Norman Conquest to about 1485
e: The Middle Ages (the medieval period) runs roughly from the Norman Conquest to the end of the Wars of the Roses in 1485.

q: What happened to King Charles I in 1649?
e: Charles I was executed in 1649, and England became a republic for a time.

q: The Crimean War of the 1850s was fought by Britain against which country?
e: Britain fought with Turkey and France against Russia in the Crimean War.

q: Which conflict in the 1980s involved Britain and Argentina over a group of South Atlantic islands?
e: The Falklands War of 1982 was fought after Argentina invaded the British Falkland Islands.

q: The scientist Sir Isaac Newton was a member of which learned society?
e: The Royal Society, one of the oldest scientific societies, counted Isaac Newton among its members.

q: The welfare state set up after 1945 was based on a report by whom?
e: The Beveridge Report of 1942 set out the plan for the welfare state, tackling the 'five giant evils'.

q: During the English Civil War, which side did the 'Cavaliers' support?
e: The Cavaliers were supporters of King Charles I.

q: The supersonic passenger aircraft Concorde was developed jointly by Britain and which country?
e: Concorde, a supersonic passenger plane, was developed jointly by Britain and France.

q: The scientist Stephen Hawking was known for his work on which subject?
e: Professor Stephen Hawking wrote 'A Brief History of Time' and studied black holes and the universe.

q: Which Welsh poet wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night'?
e: Dylan Thomas was a famous Welsh poet and writer.

q: Which Christian festival remembers the resurrection of Jesus and moves between March and April?
e: Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus Christ and takes place in March or April.

q: Pub names, Sunday roasts and fish and chips are examples of what?
e: These are part of everyday British culture and customs.

q: The BBC is funded mainly by what?
e: The BBC is a public service broadcaster funded mainly through the television licence fee.

q: Which Welsh-born actor was known for roles in classic films and a distinctive voice?
e: Richard Burton was a celebrated Welsh actor.

q: Which Scottish author wrote historical novels such as 'Ivanhoe' and 'Waverley'?
e: Sir Walter Scott was a Scottish novelist and poet, famous for works like 'Ivanhoe'.

q: What is the group of senior ministers chosen by the Prime Minister called?
e: The Cabinet is made up of about 20 senior ministers chosen by the Prime Minister.

q: In Scotland, minor criminal cases are heard in which court?
o: The Justice of the Peace Court or Sheriff Court
e: Scotland has its own courts, including Justice of the Peace Courts and Sheriff Courts for less serious cases.

q: A person who tries to influence government policy, such as an environmental group, is part of what?
e: Pressure groups try to influence government policy on particular issues.

q: The small claims procedure in the civil courts is used for what?
o: Settling minor disputes, often about money, quickly and cheaply
e: The small claims procedure handles minor civil disputes, such as faulty goods or small debts.

q: The three devolved administrations of the UK are in Scotland, Wales and where?
e: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have devolved administrations; the Isle of Man is a Crown dependency, not part of the UK.

q: If you want to stand as a candidate in an election, you generally need to be what?
o: A qualifying citizen who meets the legal requirements
A member of the House of Lords
e: Qualifying citizens who meet the legal conditions can stand for election to many public bodies.

q: Which four countries make up the United Kingdom?
o: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland
Great Britain and the Channel Islands
e: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

q: The longest river in the United Kingdom is which?
e: The River Severn is the longest river in the UK.

q: What were built in Britain during the Bronze Age?
e: Bronze Age people built round barrows and stone circles such as Stonehenge and Avebury.

q: During the Middle Ages, English kings fought a long series of wars in France known as what?
e: The Hundred Years War was a series of wars with France; the English eventually left France in the 1450s.

q: The return of the monarchy in 1660, when Charles II became king, is called what?
e: The Restoration was the return of Charles II to the throne in 1660.

q: Florence Nightingale became famous for her nursing work during which war?
e: Nightingale nursed wounded soldiers in the Crimean War and is seen as the founder of modern nursing.

q: Sir Winston Churchill, Clement Attlee and Margaret Thatcher are all examples of what?
e: All three served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.

q: The Bank of England was founded in which century to help fund government and trade?
e: The Bank of England was established in 1694.

q: In the 1960s Britain saw major changes in which areas of society?
e: The 1960s were a period of great social change, including in music, fashion and attitudes.

q: The 'Glorious Revolution' of 1688 is called 'glorious' because it was what?
e: It is called 'glorious' because power changed hands with little bloodshed in England.

q: The Festival of Britain, celebrating British achievements, was held in which year?
e: The Festival of Britain in 1951 celebrated British science, technology, design and the arts.

q: The telephone was developed by which Scottish-born inventor?
e: Alexander Graham Bell, who was born in Scotland, is credited with inventing the telephone.

q: 'The Lord of the Rings' was written by which British author?
e: J.R.R. Tolkien wrote 'The Lord of the Rings', regularly voted among Britain's best-loved books.

q: Mothering Sunday falls three weeks before which festival?
e: Mothering Sunday (Mother's Day) is the Sunday three weeks before Easter.

q: The legal age to buy alcohol in a pub or bar in the UK is usually what?
e: You usually have to be 18 to buy alcohol in the UK.

q: Which London art gallery houses a national collection of paintings in Trafalgar Square?
e: The National Gallery in Trafalgar Square holds a major collection of paintings.

q: Burns Night, celebrating a famous poet, is held on which date?
e: Burns Night, celebrating the poet Robert Burns, is held on 25 January.

q: Which 17th-century composer and organist is one of Britain's most celebrated early musicians?
e: Henry Purcell was a leading composer of the Baroque period and organist at Westminster Abbey.

q: The minister responsible for relations with other countries is called what?
e: The Foreign Secretary manages relations with foreign countries.

q: A person accused of a crime is presumed what until proven guilty?
e: In UK law a person is innocent until proven guilty.

q: The Speaker of the House of Commons is responsible for what?
o: Keeping order during debates and being politically neutral
e: The Speaker chairs debates in the Commons, keeps order and remains politically neutral.

q: You can get free, confidential legal and money advice from which type of organisation?
e: Citizens Advice provides free, independent and confidential advice on many issues.

q: Devolution means that certain powers have been given to bodies in which places?
e: Devolution transferred some powers from the UK Parliament to bodies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

q: Which of these helps protect workers from unfair treatment at work?
e: Employment law gives workers rights, for example to fair treatment, a contract and protection from discrimination.

q: What is the capital city of the United Kingdom?
e: London is the capital of the UK.

q: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have what, in addition to being part of the UK?
o: Their own devolved governments or assemblies
e: Each of these nations has devolved institutions with some of their own powers, while remaining part of the UK.

q: People of the Iron Age in Britain spoke which family of languages?
e: Iron Age people spoke Celtic languages, related to the languages still spoken in parts of Wales, Scotland and Ireland.

q: At the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, King Henry V defeated the army of which country?
e: Henry V's famous victory at Agincourt was against the French during the Hundred Years War.

q: The Great Plague of London happened in which year, shortly before the Great Fire?
e: A major outbreak of plague, the Great Plague, hit London in 1665, the year before the Great Fire of 1666.

q: The Victoria Cross, the highest award for bravery, was introduced during which conflict?
e: The Victoria Cross medal was introduced during the Crimean War.

q: The abolition of slavery, factory reforms and the expansion of the vote all took place during which era?
e: These social reforms were features of the 19th century, much of it during Victoria's reign.

q: The first Jacobite rebellion aimed to put which royal line back on the throne?
e: The Jacobites wanted to restore the Catholic Stuart line to the throne.

q: Which decade saw the UK join the European Economic Community (the forerunner of the EU)?
e: The UK joined the European Economic Community in 1973.

q: The Bill of Rights 1689 set out the powers of which body?
e: The Bill of Rights confirmed that the monarch could not rule without the consent of Parliament.

q: Which Scottish doctor shared in the discovery of insulin, used to treat diabetes?
e: Sir John Macleod was one of the scientists involved in the discovery of insulin.

q: Which sport's rules were codified in Britain and includes the famous 'Wimbledon' championship?
e: Modern tennis evolved in England, and Wimbledon is the oldest tennis tournament in the world.

q: Agatha Christie is one of the best-selling authors of all time, writing in which genre?
e: Agatha Christie wrote detective stories featuring characters such as Hercule Poirot.

q: Which festival is celebrated by Muslims and marks the end of Ramadan?
e: Eid al-Fitr celebrates the end of Ramadan, the month of fasting, for Muslims.

q: Which British mathematician and writer is sometimes called the first computer programmer?
e: Ada Lovelace worked with Charles Babbage and is regarded as a pioneer of computer programming.

q: The British Museum in London is famous for what?
o: A huge collection of objects from many cultures and periods
e: The British Museum holds artefacts from around the world and across history.

q: What food is traditionally eaten at a Burns Night supper?
e: Burns Night suppers traditionally feature haggis, served with turnips (neeps) and potatoes (tatties).

q: Robert Adam was a celebrated Scottish figure in which field?
e: Robert Adam was an influential 18th-century architect and designer.

q: Civil servants who help the government carry out its policies must be what?
o: Members of the House of Lords
e: Civil servants are politically neutral and chosen on merit; they serve whichever government is in power.

q: Who decides the verdict in a Crown Court trial?
e: In a Crown Court, the jury of 12 members decides whether the defendant is guilty, and the judge decides the sentence.

q: Which of these is a way the public can contact their MP?
o: By writing, emailing or attending their local surgery
e: People can contact their MP by letter, email, telephone or by attending a constituency surgery.

q: The right to vote in a secret ballot means what?
o: No one can be forced to say how they voted
e: Voting is by secret ballot, so no one has to say how they voted.

q: Which of these is decided by the UK Parliament for the whole UK, not by the devolved bodies?
e: Matters such as immigration, defence and foreign policy are reserved to the UK Parliament.

q: Freedom of the press in the UK means what?
o: The media can report and criticise within the law
e: A free press can report news and criticise those in power, within the limits of the law.

q: What is the capital city of Wales?
e: Cardiff is the capital of Wales.

q: What must you agree to do when you apply to become a permanent resident or citizen of the UK?
e: You agree to respect the laws, values and traditions of the UK when you apply to become a permanent resident or citizen.

q: What skill were Iron Age people in Britain able to do that earlier peoples could not?
e: The Iron Age is named for the people's ability to make tools and weapons out of iron.

q: The Magna Carta of 1215 is important because it established what principle?
o: That the king was above the law
That even the king was subject to the law
e: Magna Carta established the idea that even the king was subject to the law and had to respect certain rights.

q: The Habeas Corpus Act, guaranteeing nobody could be held unlawfully, was passed during whose reign?
e: The Habeas Corpus Act of 1679, under Charles II, meant a prisoner had the right to be brought before a court.

q: The first part of the United Kingdom to industrialise brought great wealth but also what problem?
o: Poor and crowded living and working conditions
e: Industrial towns grew rapidly, often with poor housing and dangerous working conditions.

q: The Romans named the island of Britain what?
e: The Romans called the province Britannia.

q: Bonnie Prince Charlie led a Jacobite rising in which year, ending at Culloden?
e: Charles Edward Stuart led the 1745 rising, which was crushed at Culloden in 1746.

q: The peace agreement that helped end much of the conflict in Northern Ireland is known as what?
e: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 was a key step in the Northern Ireland peace process.

q: The Act of Union 1707 created a single Parliament for Great Britain, based where?
e: After 1707 a single Parliament for Great Britain sat at Westminster in London.

q: Sir Peter Mansfield was a British scientist who helped develop which medical technology?
e: Sir Peter Mansfield helped develop the MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scanner.

q: The first modern football (association football) clubs were formed in which country?
e: Football developed in Britain in the 19th century, and the UK has four national teams.

q: Which British author created the spy character James Bond?
e: Ian Fleming wrote the James Bond novels.

q: Eid ul-Adha is a Muslim festival that remembers which event?
o: Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son for God
e: Eid ul-Adha remembers that the Prophet Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son when God asked him to.

q: Which engineer built an early mechanical computer design, the 'Analytical Engine'?
e: Charles Babbage designed early mechanical computers in the 19th century.

q: Which prize is awarded annually for the best original British visual artwork?
e: The Turner Prize is a well-known award for contemporary British visual art.

q: April Fools' Day, when people play jokes, falls on which date?
e: On 1 April people traditionally play tricks on one another until midday.

q: Which of these was a Romantic poet, alongside Wordsworth and Blake?
e: Lord Byron was one of the Romantic poets, along with Wordsworth, Blake, Keats and Shelley.

q: What is the role of the opposition in Parliament?
o: To challenge and scrutinise the government
e: The opposition's job is to hold the government to account and challenge its policies.

q: The police force in the UK is expected to be what?
o: Independent and professional, serving the public
e: The police are expected to be professional, independent and to protect the public fairly.

q: What happens at a citizenship ceremony?
o: You take an oath or affirmation and a pledge of loyalty
You are given a passport only
e: New citizens attend a ceremony and make an oath or affirmation of allegiance and a pledge to the UK.

q: What should you do if you move house, regarding your right to vote?
o: Register to vote again at your new address
e: You need to register at your new address to stay on the electoral register.

q: How often are elections for local councils usually held?
o: Regularly, on fixed cycles set by law
e: Local council elections are held regularly according to fixed legal arrangements.

q: What is the best way to deal with a disagreement with a neighbour, if talking does not work?
o: Seek help such as mediation or legal advice
e: Disputes should be resolved peacefully and lawfully, for example through mediation or legal advice.

q: Which of these is NOT part of Great Britain?
e: Great Britain refers only to England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland is part of the UK but not of Great Britain.

q: Which of these is a fundamental principle of British life?
o: A single state religion for all
e: The fundamental principles include democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance and participation in community life.

q: The first coins to be minted in Britain date from which period?
e: Some of the first coins minted in Britain, inscribed with the names of Iron Age kings, date from this period.

q: The Black Death of 1348 killed roughly what proportion of the population of England?
e: The Black Death, a form of plague, killed about a third of the population of England.

q: The overthrow of James II in 1688 and the invitation to William of Orange is known as what?
e: William of Orange was invited to invade in 1688; this peaceful change of power is called the Glorious Revolution.

q: The 'Rotten Boroughs' were reformed by which Act, which gave more people the vote?
e: The Reform Act of 1832 abolished many old abuses and greatly increased the number of people who could vote.

q: What did the Romans fail to do during their occupation of Britain?
e: The Romans never conquered the area now called Scotland, which is why Hadrian's Wall was built.

q: After Culloden, many Highlanders were forced off their land in events known as what?
e: The Highland Clearances saw many people cleared from their lands in the Scottish Highlands.

q: For how long had people been living in Britain before the last Ice Age pushed them out?
o: Tens of thousands of years, on and off
e: People came and went for tens of thousands of years as the climate changed, only settling permanently as the last Ice Age ended.

q: The British Empire grew partly through the activities of which trading company in India?
e: The East India Company played a major role in extending British influence in India.

q: The 'Clearances' that removed many people from their land took place mainly in which area?
e: The Highland Clearances in Scotland removed many families from their land, often to make way for sheep farming.

q: How many national football teams does the UK have?
e: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own national football team.

q: The novel '1984' and 'Animal Farm' were written by which author?
e: George Orwell wrote '1984' and 'Animal Farm'.

q: Diwali, the festival of lights, lasts for about how long?
e: Diwali lasts for five days and is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs.

q: The discovery of the structure of DNA involved the X-ray work of which British scientist?
e: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography was crucial to discovering the structure of DNA.

q: The 'Angel of the North' sculpture stands near which city?
e: Antony Gormley's 'Angel of the North' stands near Gateshead in north-east England.

q: What do children traditionally do on the evening of 31 October (Hallowe'en)?
o: Dress up and go 'trick or treating'
e: On Hallowe'en children dress in costumes, and 'trick or treating' is popular.

q: Sir Francis Chichester is remembered as the first person to do what in 1966-67?
e: Sir Francis Chichester was the first person to sail single-handed around the world.

q: The 'shadow cabinet' is made up of senior members of which group?
e: The leader of the opposition appoints senior colleagues to a shadow cabinet to mirror the government ministers.

q: If you think the police have treated you unfairly, what can you do?
o: Make a complaint, which will be investigated
e: You can make a formal complaint against the police, and there are independent bodies to investigate.

q: Which of these is a fundamental right protected in the UK?
o: The right to a fair trial
The right to break the law
The right to ignore court orders
e: The right to a fair trial is one of the fundamental rights and freedoms in the UK.

q: Which of these is a reason you might be excused from jury service?
o: You do not want to do it
A good reason such as serious illness
You are too busy at work generally
e: You can be excused from jury service only for a good reason, such as illness; you cannot simply refuse.

q: What is the main role of a Member of Parliament (MP)?
o: To run a government department always
To represent their constituents and consider new laws
e: MPs represent the people in their constituency, debate and pass laws, and scrutinise the government.

q: Which of these is a benefit of registering to vote, besides voting?
o: It can help when applying for credit
It removes the need to pay tax
It exempts you from jury service
e: Being on the electoral register can also help when applying for things such as credit.

q: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are governed how?
o: As full parts of the UK
As Crown dependencies with their own governments
As independent countries in the UN
e: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies; they are not part of the UK and have their own governments.

q: What are you taking part in when you read the handbook and take the test?
o: Becoming a permanent resident or citizen
e: The test and handbook are part of the process of becoming a permanent resident or citizen of the UK.

q: Why was Julius Caesar's attempt to invade Britain in 55 BC significant despite failing?
o: It marked the beginning of a written record of events in Britain
e: Caesar's unsuccessful invasion is often seen as the start of the written record of events in Britain.

q: In the Middle Ages, Parliament began to develop into two separate parts known as what?
o: The House of Lords and the House of Commons
e: Parliament developed into the House of Lords and the House of Commons during the medieval period.

q: William III and his wife Mary ruled jointly after 1688. Mary was the daughter of which deposed king?
e: Mary was the Protestant daughter of the Catholic James II, who had been overthrown.

q: Working men and some reformers campaigned in the 1830s and 1840s for voting rights under which movement?
e: The Chartists campaigned for all men to have the vote and for other political reforms.

q: After the Romans left, which period is sometimes called the 'Dark Ages'?
e: The years after the Roman departure, during the Anglo-Saxon settlement, are sometimes called the Dark Ages.

q: The Seven Years War and later conflicts helped Britain gain control of large parts of which country?
e: Britain gained control over large parts of India, partly through the East India Company.

q: The builders of Stonehenge are thought to have come from which period?
o: The Stone Age and Bronze Age
e: Stonehenge was built over many centuries during the late Stone Age and Bronze Age.

q: Captain James Cook is famous for exploring and mapping which region?
e: Captain Cook charted the coast of Australia and explored the Pacific in the 18th century.

q: During the reign of which queen did Britain become the most powerful industrial and trading nation?
e: Under Queen Victoria, Britain became the world's leading industrial and trading power.

q: The Open Championship is a major tournament in which sport, which developed in Scotland?
e: Golf originated in Scotland in the 15th century; St Andrews is known as its home.

q: The Brontë sisters, who wrote 'Jane Eyre' and 'Wuthering Heights', were from which part of England?
e: The Brontë sisters lived in Yorkshire and wrote classic novels in the 19th century.

q: What does the Christian festival of Lent lead up to?
e: Lent is the 40 days before Easter, traditionally a period of fasting that begins on Ash Wednesday.

q: Which fossil hunter from Lyme Regis made important discoveries in the early 19th century?
e: Mary Anning found important fossils that helped develop the understanding of prehistoric life.

q: The Eden Project, with giant greenhouse biomes, is located in which county?
e: The Eden Project in Cornwall houses plants from around the world in huge domes.

q: Bonfire Night on 5 November includes fireworks and remembers which event?
o: The end of the Second World War
e: Bonfire Night marks the failure of the 1605 plot to blow up Parliament.

q: Baroness Tanni Grey-Thompson is one of Britain's most successful athletes in which arena?
e: Dame Tanni Grey-Thompson won many gold medals as a Paralympic wheelchair racer.

q: Which of these powers is devolved to the Scottish Parliament?
e: Devolved matters such as education and health are decided by the Scottish Parliament, while defence and foreign affairs stay with the UK Parliament.

q: Which of these must you have by law to drive a car in the UK?
o: A valid driving licence, insurance and (for older cars) an MOT
e: To drive you need a valid licence, motor insurance and, for cars over a certain age, a valid MOT certificate.

q: The House of Commons and the House of Lords together make up what?
e: Parliament is made up of the House of Commons and the House of Lords, along with the monarch.

q: Taxes collected by the government pay for which of these?
o: Public services such as roads, schools and the armed forces
e: Taxes fund public services including health, education, roads, defence and welfare.

q: Which of these can an MP help a constituent with?
o: Taking up a problem with a government department
e: MPs can take up constituents' concerns, including problems with public bodies and government departments.

q: Who is responsible for making sure children of school age attend school?
e: Parents and carers are responsible for ensuring their children receive a suitable education.

q: Which body is responsible for defence and foreign affairs across the whole UK?
e: Powers such as defence and foreign affairs are not devolved and remain with the UK Parliament.

q: Which of these is a responsibility you accept as a citizen or permanent resident?
o: To vote for a particular party
e: Responsibilities include treating others with fairness, looking after yourself and your family, and looking after the area you live in.

q: Which British queen of the Iceni tribe led a revolt against the Romans?
e: Boudicca, queen of the Iceni in eastern England, led an uprising against the Romans and is remembered with a statue on Westminster Bridge.

q: Which war between the royal houses of Lancaster and York was fought in the 15th century?
e: The Wars of the Roses were fought between the House of Lancaster (red rose) and the House of York (white rose).

q: Supporters of James II who wanted to restore his line to the throne were known as what?
e: The Jacobites supported James II and his descendants; they were finally defeated at Culloden in 1746.

q: The women who campaigned for the right to vote in the early 20th century were known as what?
e: The suffragettes campaigned, sometimes using civil disobedience, for women's right to vote.

q: The famous illuminated manuscript of the Gospels was produced on which island off Northumberland?
e: The Lindisfarne Gospels were produced at the monastery on Lindisfarne (Holy Island).

q: The loss of which colonies occurred after the American War of Independence?
e: Britain lost its thirteen American colonies, which became the United States, in 1776 onwards.

q: What happened to Britain's connection with mainland Europe about 10,000 years ago?
o: It was separated by rising seas forming the Channel
e: As the Ice Age ended, sea levels rose and Britain became separated from the continent.

q: The Industrial Revolution led many people to move from the countryside to where?
e: Industrialisation drew people from rural areas into expanding towns and cities to work in factories.

q: Which conflict of 1899-1902 was fought by Britain in southern Africa?
e: The Boer War was fought in South Africa at the turn of the 20th century.

q: Which annual rowing race is contested between the universities of Oxford and Cambridge?
e: The University Boat Race between Oxford and Cambridge has been held on the Thames since 1829.

q: Which composer wrote 'The Enigma Variations' and the 'Pomp and Circumstance Marches'?
e: Sir Edward Elgar is famous for the Enigma Variations and the Pomp and Circumstance Marches.

q: The day before Lent begins, when pancakes are traditionally eaten, is called what?
e: Shrove Tuesday, or Pancake Day, is the day before the start of Lent.

q: The economist John Maynard Keynes is famous for his ideas about what?
e: John Maynard Keynes developed influential economic theories, especially about government and the economy.

q: Which famous naval ship, HMS Victory, is preserved at which city?
e: HMS Victory, Nelson's flagship, is preserved at Portsmouth.

q: Which festival of lights is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains?
e: Diwali, the festival of lights, is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains.

q: The novelist Kazuo Ishiguro, a British author, has won which major literary prize?
e: Kazuo Ishiguro, author of 'The Remains of the Day', won the Booker Prize.

q: The Welsh devolved law-making body is based where?
e: The Welsh devolved government and law-making body are based in Cardiff.

q: Income tax is paid on what?
o: Earnings from employment, self-employment, pensions and some other income
e: Income tax is paid on money earned from work, profits, pensions and some other income.

q: How are Members of the Scottish Parliament chosen?
o: Elected by the people of Scotland
e: MSPs are elected by voters in Scotland.

q: What is the role of local councillors?
o: To represent people and make decisions on local services
e: Local councillors are elected to represent their area and make decisions about local services.

q: Who formally opens the new session of Parliament each year?
e: The monarch opens each new session of Parliament and reads out the government's plans.

q: The three main traditional political parties in the UK are the Conservatives, Labour and which other?
e: The Conservative, Labour and Liberal Democrat parties are the three largest traditional UK-wide parties.

q: What is the longest-distance walk, roughly, between the two ends of the island of Great Britain?
o: From John O'Groats to Land's End
e: John O'Groats in the north of Scotland to Land's End in the south-west of England is the length of the island, about 870 miles.

q: What does the UK offer in return for respecting its laws and values?
o: Freedom of speech, a fair trial and equal treatment
e: In return, the UK offers freedoms such as freedom of belief, freedom of speech, a fair trial and equal rights.

q: Roman Britain became part of the Roman Empire and remained so for how long?
e: Britain was part of the Roman Empire for about 400 years.

q: The Wars of the Roses ended in 1485 with victory for whom at Bosworth Field?
e: Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth Field and became King Henry VII, the first Tudor king.

q: The Act of Union of 1707 joined which two kingdoms?
e: The Act of Union of 1707 joined England (with Wales) and Scotland to create the Kingdom of Great Britain.

q: Emmeline Pankhurst founded which organisation to campaign for women's votes?
o: The Women's Social and Political Union
e: Emmeline Pankhurst set up the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903.

q: Which king is said to have ordered the building of a great network of defensive forts and burhs against the Vikings?
e: Alfred the Great organised defences, including fortified towns, against the Vikings.

q: Admiral Nelson died at which battle in 1805, defeating the French and Spanish fleets?
e: Nelson won the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 but was killed during it; his column stands in Trafalgar Square.

q: Which people built hill forts across Britain during the Iron Age?
e: Iron Age Celtic peoples built hill forts, some of which can still be seen today.

q: Trade unions were formed during the Industrial era to do what?
o: Protect the interests and rights of workers
e: Trade unions developed to improve pay and working conditions for workers.

q: The invention of the World Wide Web and work on DNA show the UK's continuing strength in what?
e: The UK has a long record of scientific discovery and innovation, continuing into modern times.

q: The Six Nations rugby championship is played in which code of rugby?
e: The Six Nations is a rugby union competition between England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy.

q: Which composer, who wrote the opera 'Peter Grimes', helped found classical music festivals in the 20th century?
e: Benjamin Britten is best known for operas such as 'Peter Grimes' and 'Billy Budd'.

q: Which flower is traditionally worn on Remembrance Day to remember those who died in wars?
e: A red poppy is worn around Remembrance Day, 11 November, to remember those who died in conflicts.

q: The 'Harry Potter' series of books was written by which British author?
e: J.K. Rowling wrote the hugely popular Harry Potter novels.

q: The Lake District, the Brecon Beacons and the Cairngorms are all examples of what?
e: These are national parks, protected areas of countryside in different parts of the UK.

q: The Jewish festival that lasts eight days and involves lighting candles is called what?
e: Hanukkah is a Jewish festival lasting eight days, during which candles are lit.

q: The Commonwealth Games, in which UK nations compete separately, are held how often?
e: The Commonwealth Games are held every four years, with England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland competing separately.

q: The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at which location in Belfast?
e: The Northern Ireland Assembly sits at Stormont in Belfast.

q: Everyone working in the UK must have which number for tax and National Insurance?
e: A National Insurance number is a unique personal number used to record contributions.

q: A government is usually formed by the party that does what at a general election?
o: Wins the most seats in the House of Commons
e: The party (or coalition) with a majority of seats in the Commons normally forms the government.

q: How are most local councillors chosen?
e: Local councillors are elected by residents of the local area.

q: What is a 'manifesto'?
o: A statement of what a political party will do if elected
e: A manifesto sets out the policies a political party promises to follow if it wins an election.

q: Which of these is a minister in the Cabinet?
e: Cabinet ministers include the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Home Secretary and the Foreign Secretary.

q: Which of these is a Crown dependency?
e: The Isle of Man is a Crown dependency. The Falklands, Gibraltar and Bermuda are British overseas territories.

q: Looking for work when unemployed is best described as what?
o: Part of taking responsibility for yourself and your family
A role only for young people
e: Looking after yourself and your family, including looking for work when unemployed, is one of the responsibilities of living in the UK.

q: Hadrian's Wall was built on the orders of which Roman emperor?
e: The Emperor Hadrian ordered the wall built to keep out the Picts of what is now Scotland.

q: Which king established the Church of England after the Pope refused to annul his marriage?
e: Henry VIII broke away from the Church of Rome and set up the Church of England so he could divorce Catherine of Aragon.

q: Who is generally regarded as the first Prime Minister, serving from 1721?
e: Sir Robert Walpole, in effect the first Prime Minister, held power from 1721 to 1742.

q: The First World War began in which year?
e: The First World War began in 1914 and ended in 1918.

q: Edward I built a series of impressive stone castles to control which country?
e: Edward I built castles such as Caernarfon and Conwy to control Wales after conquering it.

q: The Duke of Wellington, who defeated Napoleon at Waterloo, later became what?
e: The Duke of Wellington went on to become Prime Minister.

q: What was one lasting Roman contribution to Britain?
o: A network of roads and towns
e: The Romans built roads and towns, some of which are still the basis of settlements and routes today.

q: The 19th-century social reformer known for improving conditions for factory children was associated with which kind of law?
e: A series of Factory Acts gradually improved conditions and limited working hours, especially for children.

q: Which structure did the Romans famously build across northern England?
e: Hadrian's Wall was built across northern England on the orders of the Emperor Hadrian.

q: In which year did London host the Olympic and Paralympic Games, its third time hosting?
e: London hosted the Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2012, having also hosted in 1908 and 1948.

q: The 'Last Night of the Proms' is the final concert in a famous series of concerts held mainly where?
e: The BBC Proms are a series of concerts held mainly at the Royal Albert Hall in London.

q: The patron saint of England is who, celebrated on 23 April?
e: St George is the patron saint of England; his day is 23 April.

q: Which author wrote children's books such as 'Charlie and the Chocolate Factory'?
e: Roald Dahl wrote many well-loved children's books.

q: Loch Ness, famous for its legendary monster, is located in which country?
e: Loch Ness is a large freshwater loch in the Scottish Highlands.

q: The Notting Hill Carnival in London celebrates the culture of which communities?
e: The Notting Hill Carnival is a celebration of Caribbean culture and one of Europe's biggest street festivals.

q: Which annual event sees people in Scotland celebrate the poet Robert Burns?
e: Burns Night, on 25 January, celebrates the life and work of the poet Robert Burns.

q: Who is allowed to attend debates in Parliament and watch from the public galleries?
e: The public can watch debates from the galleries in both Houses of Parliament.

q: Local services such as rubbish collection and schools are provided by which bodies?
e: Local councils provide many day-to-day services and are funded partly by council tax.

q: What is a coalition government?
o: A government formed by two or more parties working together
A government with no Prime Minister
A government run by the Lords
e: A coalition is formed when two or more parties join to govern, usually because no single party has a majority.

q: Charities and voluntary groups are an important part of what?
o: Community and public life in the UK
e: Charities and voluntary organisations play a major role in UK community life.

q: What is the main opposition party's leader known as?
e: The Leader of the Opposition heads the largest party that is not in government.

q: What is 'proportional representation', used in some UK elections?
o: A system where seats reflect the share of votes a party wins
A system where the king chooses MPs
A system used only in courts
e: Proportional representation, used for some devolved and other elections, allocates seats more in line with the share of votes.

q: Gibraltar and the Falkland Islands are examples of what?
e: They are British overseas territories, linked to the UK but not part of it.

q: Which of these shows respect for the environment, a value shared by UK residents?
e: Looking after the environment, recycling and not wasting water or energy is part of being a good citizen.

q: What religion had become widespread in Roman Britain by the 3rd and 4th centuries?
e: By the 3rd and 4th centuries AD Christianity was becoming established in Britain.

q: How many wives did King Henry VIII have?
e: Henry VIII married six times: Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard and Catherine Parr.

q: The period in the 18th century of new ideas about politics, science and philosophy is called what?
e: The Enlightenment saw great advances in science, philosophy and ideas about society.

q: The Allied powers in the First World War did NOT include which of these?
e: Germany was one of the Central Powers; Britain, France, Russia and later the USA were among the Allies.

q: The 'Auld Alliance' in the Middle Ages was between Scotland and which country?
e: Scotland and France formed the 'Auld Alliance' against England.

q: Britain's trade and manufacturing grew so much in the 19th century it was called what?
e: Britain was known as 'the workshop of the world' during the Industrial Revolution.

q: The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were eventually united in part through the efforts of kings from which kingdom?
e: The kings of Wessex, including Alfred the Great, played a major role in resisting the Vikings and unifying England.

q: What did the Representation of the People Acts gradually do over the 19th and early 20th centuries?
o: Extend the right to vote to more people
e: A series of reform acts gradually extended the vote to more of the adult population.
