q: Offa's Dyke, an earthwork roughly marking a border, lies between England and which country?
e: Offa's Dyke was built roughly along the border between England and Wales.

q: The Paralympic Games have their origins at which UK hospital?
e: The Paralympic movement began at Stoke Mandeville hospital, where Dr Ludwig Guttmann organised sport for patients.

q: Which four-member band from Liverpool became one of the most successful pop groups of the 1960s?
e: The Beatles, from Liverpool, are among the most influential pop groups of all time.

q: The national flower of Scotland is which plant?
e: The thistle is the national flower of Scotland.

q: Beatrix Potter is famous for writing and illustrating what?
o: Children's stories such as 'The Tale of Peter Rabbit'
e: Beatrix Potter created children's stories with animal characters, such as Peter Rabbit.

q: The 'Proms' and the Edinburgh Festival are examples of events in which category?
e: These are major arts festivals held in the UK each year.

q: The Edinburgh Festival, held each summer, is best known for what?
e: The Edinburgh Festival and its 'Fringe' feature arts, theatre and comedy from around the world.

q: Morris dancing and maypole dancing are examples of what?
e: Morris dancing and dancing around a maypole are traditional English folk customs.

q: What does the 'first past the post' system mean for a constituency?
o: Every candidate wins a share of seats
The candidate with the most votes becomes the MP
e: Under first past the post, the candidate who gets the most votes in a constituency is elected.

q: Council tax helps to pay for what?
o: Local services such as rubbish collection, roads and libraries
e: Council tax is a local tax that helps pay for services provided by local authorities.

q: Which of these is NOT a role of the monarch?
o: Representing the UK on ceremonial occasions
Acting as head of the Commonwealth
e: The monarch has a ceremonial role; day-to-day government is run by the Prime Minister and ministers.

q: Which of these is an example of volunteering?
o: Helping at a local school or hospital for free
e: Volunteering means giving your time for free to help others or a good cause.

q: Which of these is an example of 'the rule of law'?
o: Important people being above the law
The same laws applying to everyone, including the government
e: The rule of law means laws apply equally to everyone, including those who govern.

q: The way the UK is governed is based on which of these, even though there is no single written constitution?
o: Laws, conventions and key historic documents
e: The UK constitution is made up of laws, conventions and important documents such as Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights.

q: Around what fraction of the UK population lives in England?
e: England has by far the largest population, more than 80 per cent of the UK total.

q: Treating others with fairness is an example of what?
e: Treating others with fairness is one of the values and responsibilities expected of those living in the UK.

q: The Anglo-Saxons came to Britain from which region?
o: Northern Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands
e: The Angles, Saxons and Jutes came from what is now northern Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands.

q: Which of Henry VIII's wives was the mother of Edward VI?
e: Jane Seymour gave Henry the male heir he wanted, the future Edward VI, but died shortly afterwards.

q: Which Scottish economist and philosopher of the Enlightenment wrote 'The Wealth of Nations'?
e: Adam Smith developed ideas about economics that are still referred to today.

q: The Easter Rising, an armed rebellion against British rule, took place in Dublin in which year?
e: The Easter Rising of 1916 in Dublin was part of the struggle for Irish independence.

q: William Wallace and Robert the Bruce are famous for fighting for whose independence?
e: Both were leaders in the struggle for Scottish independence against England.

q: The engineer who built many railways, tunnels and the Clifton Suspension Bridge was who?
e: Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the Great Western Railway and the Clifton Suspension Bridge among many works.

q: The Normans introduced which language to the royal court after 1066?
e: Norman French became the language of the ruling class after the Conquest.

q: Which two world wars had the greatest impact on Britain in the 20th century?
o: The First and Second World Wars
The Hundred Years War and Civil War
e: The First World War (1914-18) and the Second World War (1939-45) deeply affected Britain.

q: Which scientist developed the theory of evolution by natural selection?
e: Charles Darwin, author of 'On the Origin of Species', developed the theory of evolution.

q: Which Formula 1 driver has been one of Britain's most successful, winning multiple world championships?
e: Sir Lewis Hamilton is one of the most successful Formula 1 racing drivers.

q: Which British painter is famous for landscapes such as 'The Fighting Temeraire'?
e: J.M.W. Turner was an influential landscape painter; the Turner Prize is named after him.

q: The national flower of England is which plant?
e: The rose is the national flower of England.

q: Which British scientist is credited with the discovery of hydrogen and work on gases?
e: Henry Cavendish discovered hydrogen; the UK has many notable scientists.

q: Which Scottish-born scientist is associated with the development of the telephone?
e: Alexander Graham Bell, born in Edinburgh, is credited with developing the telephone.

q: The Highland Games in Scotland include traditional events such as what?
o: Tossing the caber and Highland dancing
e: Highland Games feature traditional Scottish events like tossing the caber, as well as dancing and music.

q: Which of these is a famous British car marque, reflecting the UK's engineering heritage?
e: Rolls-Royce is a famous British manufacturer, reflecting the country's engineering tradition.

q: MEPs used to be elected to which body before the UK left it?
e: Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) were elected while the UK was a member of the European Union.

q: Which of these is a legal requirement for parents regarding children's education?
o: Children must attend a private school
Children must receive a suitable full-time education from age 5 to 16
e: Parents must ensure children of compulsory school age receive a suitable full-time education.

q: Bills must be approved by both Houses and then receive what before becoming law?
e: A proposed law (a Bill) becomes an Act once it has passed both Houses and received Royal Assent from the monarch.

q: Recycling household waste is an example of taking responsibility for what?
e: Looking after the environment, including recycling, is a shared responsibility.

q: In the UK, people are free to practise which of these?
e: People in the UK are free to follow any religion or none, a key freedom.

q: Which of these can help you if you have a problem at work?
e: Trade unions and organisations such as Citizens Advice can help with problems at work.

q: Which of these is the official name of the country?
o: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
e: The full official name is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

q: Which of these freedoms is offered to people living in the UK?
e: The UK offers freedoms including freedom of speech, freedom of belief and the right to a fair trial.

q: Which language is modern English largely based on?
e: The Anglo-Saxon language is the basis of English as it is spoken today.

q: Which of Henry VIII's wives was executed after Anne Boleyn, having also been accused of taking lovers?
e: Catherine Howard, like Anne Boleyn, was executed for taking lovers.

q: The Industrial Revolution refers to the rapid development of what?
o: Industry, with new machines and factories
e: The Industrial Revolution was the rapid growth of industry, powered by machinery, in the 18th and 19th centuries.

q: In 1921 a treaty led to the division of Ireland, with the south becoming what?
e: The Irish Free State became a self-governing dominion in 1922, while Northern Ireland remained part of the UK.

q: The 'Canterbury Tales' by Geoffrey Chaucer were written in which language?
e: Chaucer wrote 'The Canterbury Tales' in English, helping to establish it as a literary language.

q: The Great Exhibition of 1851 was held in which London building?
e: The Great Exhibition took place in the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, showcasing industry and invention.

q: Castles such as the White Tower at the Tower of London were first built by whom?
e: The Normans built castles, including the White Tower, to control the country after 1066.

q: The National Health Service was created in which year?
e: The NHS was founded in 1948 as part of the post-war welfare state.

q: Alexander Fleming is famous for discovering what?
e: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic, in 1928.

q: Dame Kelly Holmes won two Olympic gold medals in 2004 in which sport?
e: Dame Kelly Holmes won gold in the 800m and 1500m at the 2004 Olympics.

q: Thomas Gainsborough was famous for painting what?
e: Thomas Gainsborough was a leading portrait painter of the 18th century.

q: The daffodil and the leek are national symbols of which country?
e: The daffodil and the leek are both associated with Wales.

q: Michael Faraday made important discoveries in which field?
e: Michael Faraday's work on electricity and magnetism was hugely influential.

q: Sir Alexander Fleming's discovery of penicillin was important because it was the first what?
e: Penicillin was the first antibiotic, used to treat bacterial infections.

q: Which of these is a traditional pub game in the UK?
e: Darts is a popular traditional pub game across the UK.

q: The 'Gherkin' and 'The Shard' are examples of what in London?
e: The Gherkin and The Shard are well-known modern skyscrapers in London.

q: Who can register to vote in UK elections?
o: Citizens aged 18 or over who are on the electoral register and qualify
Only people born in the UK
e: To vote, you must be 18 or over, a qualifying citizen (UK, Irish or Commonwealth) and registered on the electoral register.

q: Volunteering and helping in the community is encouraged as what?
o: A valued way of taking part in society
e: Volunteering is seen as an important and valued way of contributing to the community.

q: A proposed new law being debated in Parliament is called what?
e: A Bill is a proposed law; once passed and given Royal Assent it becomes an Act.

q: Which of these helps keep communities safe and is encouraged?
o: Taking the law into your own hands
e: Neighbourhood Watch schemes help neighbours work together to prevent crime.

q: The highest criminal court for the most serious cases in Scotland is the what?
e: Scotland has its own courts; the High Court of Justiciary deals with the most serious criminal cases there.

q: What must employers not do under UK equality law?
o: Discriminate against people because of a protected characteristic
e: Employers must not discriminate against people because of characteristics such as race, sex, religion, age or disability.

q: The currency of the UK is what?
e: The currency of the UK is the pound sterling, symbol £.

q: Why is it important to learn English or a UK language?
o: It helps you take a full part in society and is needed to become a citizen
It replaces the need to work
e: Speaking and reading English (or Welsh or Scottish Gaelic) helps you integrate and is required to become a permanent resident or citizen.

q: Saint Patrick, patron saint of Ireland, is associated with spreading what?
e: St Patrick helped spread Christianity in Ireland and became its patron saint.

q: Which Tudor queen was a devout Catholic who had many Protestants executed, earning a grim nickname?
e: Mary, a devout Catholic, persecuted Protestants and became known as 'Bloody Mary'.

q: Before the Industrial Revolution, most people in Britain worked in what?
e: Most people worked in farming before the Industrial Revolution moved many into factories and towns.

q: The worldwide economic downturn that caused mass unemployment in the 1930s is called what?
e: The Great Depression of the 1930s brought high unemployment, especially in industrial areas.

q: In Scotland, poets writing in the 15th century and later in the Scots language were known as what?
e: Poets writing in Scots, such as those at the Scottish court, were known as 'makars'.

q: Who was Queen Victoria's husband, who helped organise the Great Exhibition?
e: Prince Albert was Victoria's husband and a keen supporter of science and the arts.

q: During the Middle Ages, who held most of the land under the feudal system?
o: The king, who granted land to nobles in return for service
e: Under feudalism, the king owned the land and granted it to nobles in exchange for help and military service.

q: The UK and other countries formed which defensive alliance in 1949?
e: NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization) was formed in 1949.

q: The structure of DNA was discovered at a UK university by Crick, Watson and colleagues. In which city was much of this work done?
e: Francis Crick and James Watson worked out the structure of DNA while working at Cambridge.

q: Bradley Wiggins became the first Briton to win which race in 2012?
e: Sir Bradley Wiggins was the first Briton to win the Tour de France cycle race.

q: Which living British artist is known for colourful paintings and is one of the most influential of his generation?
e: David Hockney contributed to the 'pop art' movement and remains a very influential artist.

q: Which famous prehistoric monument stands on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire?
e: Stonehenge is a World Heritage Site and one of the most famous prehistoric monuments in the world.

q: Which horse-racing event is attended by the Royal Family and known for its dress code?
e: Royal Ascot is a famous horse-racing meeting attended by members of the Royal Family.

q: The mathematician and code-breaker Alan Turing worked during the Second World War at which site?
e: Alan Turing worked at Bletchley Park, breaking enemy codes.

q: Afternoon tea, with tea and small cakes, is an example of what?
e: Afternoon tea is a well-known British social custom.

q: The poet Wilfred Owen and others wrote powerfully about the experience of what?
e: War poets such as Wilfred Owen wrote about their experiences in the First World War.

q: The document listing people entitled to vote is called what?
e: The electoral register lists everyone who is registered and entitled to vote.

q: Treating others with respect and not discriminating against them is required by which law?
e: The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination on grounds such as race, sex, disability, religion and age.

q: Which of these can you do if you are 18 or over and eligible?
o: Sit in the House of Lords automatically
e: Qualifying citizens aged 18 or over can register and vote in general elections.

q: The UK left which organisation following a referendum held in 2016?
e: In a 2016 referendum the UK voted to leave the European Union.

q: Which of these must a landlord generally provide to a tenant?
o: A safe property and a tenancy agreement
e: Landlords have legal duties, including keeping the property safe and providing a tenancy agreement.

q: Which of these is a way of taking an active part in the democratic process?
o: Standing as a candidate or campaigning on an issue
e: Standing for election, campaigning, joining a party and voting are all ways of taking part in democracy.

q: How many pence are there in a pound?
e: There are 100 pence (100p) in a pound (£1).

q: Which of these is part of 'participation in community life', a fundamental principle?
e: Taking part in community life, such as volunteering, is one of the fundamental principles of British life.

q: Which monk wrote an early history of England and is known as the 'Venerable Bede'?
e: The Venerable Bede was an Anglo-Saxon monk famous for writing an early history of England.

q: Under which queen did England become a strongly Protestant country and defeat the Spanish Armada?
e: Elizabeth I re-established the Church of England and, in 1588, her navy defeated the Spanish Armada.

q: Richard Arkwright is remembered for improving efficiency in which industry?
e: Arkwright is famous for improving the efficiency of textile machinery and running factories.

q: Who became Prime Minister in 1940 and led Britain through much of the Second World War?
e: Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in 1940 and is remembered for his wartime leadership.

q: Printing was introduced to England in the 15th century by whom?
e: William Caxton set up the first printing press in England.

q: The idea of a national police force in Britain is linked to which Home Secretary and later PM?
e: Sir Robert Peel set up the first modern police force; officers were nicknamed 'bobbies' after him.

q: Which rebellion in 1381, partly over taxes, is known as the Peasants' Revolt?
o: A rising of ordinary people against high taxes
e: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was a rising of ordinary people, partly against a poll tax.

q: The break-up of the British Empire after the Second World War led to the growth of what?
e: As former colonies became independent, many joined the Commonwealth.

q: Which Scottish scientist cloned the first mammal, 'Dolly the Sheep'?
e: Dolly the Sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, was created by a team including Sir Ian Wilmut in Scotland.

q: The Ashes is a famous cricket contest between England and which country?
e: The Ashes is a long-running Test cricket series between England and Australia.

q: The Proms, the Edinburgh Festival and the Eisteddfod are all examples of what?
e: These are well-known cultural festivals held in different parts of the UK.

q: The Lake District, famous for its scenery, is in which part of England?
e: The Lake District is England's largest national park, in the north-west.

q: The Derby, a famous horse race, is held at which racecourse?
e: The Derby is run at Epsom and is one of the most famous flat races.

q: Which famous naturalist sailed on HMS Beagle and developed the theory of evolution?
e: Charles Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle contributed to his theory of evolution by natural selection.

q: The 'Welsh Assembly' building (the Senedd) is located in which city?
e: The Welsh devolved institutions are based in Cardiff, the capital of Wales.

q: What kind of democracy does the UK have?
e: The UK is a parliamentary democracy with the monarch as head of state.

q: How can you register to vote if you are eligible?
o: By contacting your local council electoral registration office or registering online
You are registered automatically at birth
e: You can register through your local electoral registration office or online via the official government website.

q: Which of these is protected from discrimination under UK equality law?
o: People regardless of race, religion, sex, age or disability
e: Discrimination because of age, disability, sex, race, religion, sexual orientation and other characteristics is unlawful.

q: The MP who chairs debates and keeps order in the House of Commons is the what?
e: The Speaker keeps order in the Commons and must be politically neutral.

q: A vote in which the public decides a single important question is called what?
e: A referendum is a vote on a single issue put to the whole electorate.

q: What is the purpose of the civil courts?
o: To settle disputes between people or organisations
e: Civil courts resolve disputes, for example about money, property or contracts, rather than punishing crimes.

q: The electoral register is used to list who is entitled to do what?
e: The electoral register lists the people who are registered and entitled to vote.

q: Which of these languages is a recognised language of Scotland, besides English?
e: Scottish Gaelic is spoken in parts of Scotland; Welsh is spoken in Wales.

q: Respecting the rights of others, including those you disagree with, is an example of what value?
e: Tolerance of other people and their beliefs is a core British value.

q: The Vikings first came to Britain in AD 789 for what purpose?
o: To raid coastal towns and take goods and slaves
e: The Vikings came from Denmark and Norway, first raiding coastal towns for goods and slaves.

q: Elizabeth I never married and so had no what?
e: Elizabeth I had no children, so the throne passed to her cousin's son, James VI of Scotland.

q: The spread of railways in the 19th century was made possible by whose work on steam locomotives?
e: George Stephenson and his son Robert pioneered the railway locomotives that transformed transport.

q: Winston Churchill was voted the greatest ever Briton in a 2002 poll and is known for what?
e: Churchill is remembered for his inspiring wartime speeches and leadership during the Second World War.

q: The 'Mary Rose' was a famous warship that sank during the reign of which king?
e: The Mary Rose was Henry VIII's warship, which sank in 1545 and was later raised from the seabed.

q: Which two politicians dominated British politics for much of the later 19th century?
e: William Gladstone (Liberal) and Benjamin Disraeli (Conservative) were leading rivals in Victorian politics.

q: The Hundred Years War eventually ended with the English losing almost all their land where?
e: By the 1450s the English had lost nearly all their lands in France.

q: Which decade saw significant immigration to the UK from Commonwealth countries to help rebuild after the war?
e: In the 1950s people were invited from the West Indies, India, Pakistan and elsewhere to help fill labour shortages.

q: Sir Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist, is credited with inventing what?
e: Sir Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989.

q: Sir Ian Botham was a famous player in which sport?
e: Sir Ian Botham captained the English cricket team and held a number of records.

q: The Mercury Music Prize is awarded each year for the best what?
o: Album by a UK or Irish act
e: The Mercury Music Prize is awarded for the best album from the UK and Ireland.

q: Snowdonia (Eryri) National Park, with the mountain Snowdon, is in which country?
e: Snowdonia is a national park in Wales containing Snowdon, the highest mountain in Wales.

q: The Wimbledon tennis championships are played on which surface?
e: Wimbledon is famous for being played on grass courts.

q: Which British author wrote 'A Christmas Carol'?
e: Charles Dickens wrote 'A Christmas Carol', among many other novels.

q: Which famous clock tower stands at the Houses of Parliament in London?
e: 'Big Ben' is the nickname of the great bell; the tower that houses it is the Elizabeth Tower.

q: Who is the head of state of the UK?
e: The monarch is the head of state, while the Prime Minister is the head of government.

q: Which of these is a way citizens can take part in democracy between elections?
o: Joining a pressure group or charity
e: Getting involved in pressure groups, political parties, charities and community groups is a way of taking part.

q: The United Kingdom is a member of which international defence alliance?
e: The UK is a member of NATO, an alliance of countries that agree to defend one another.

q: Which group ensures MPs attend and vote in line with their party?
e: Party whips organise MPs and encourage them to attend and vote with their party.

q: Which of these is a duty of everyone living in the UK?
e: Obeying the law is a basic duty of everyone living in the UK.

q: Who can be asked to serve on a jury?
o: Eligible members of the public on the electoral register
e: People on the electoral register who meet the requirements can be called for jury service.

q: A person who is found guilty of a crime may receive what from the court?
o: A sentence, such as a fine or imprisonment
e: A court can impose a sentence on someone found guilty, such as a fine, community service or prison.

q: A dialect of English spoken in parts of Scotland is known as what?
e: Scots is spoken in some parts of Scotland alongside English and Scottish Gaelic.

q: Which of these is a benefit the UK offers those who respect its values?
o: A fair trial and equal treatment under the law
e: The UK offers fairness, equal treatment and a fair trial to those who live by its laws and values.

q: Which Anglo-Saxon king defeated the Vikings and allowed some to stay in the Danelaw?
e: King Alfred the Great defeated the Vikings but allowed some to remain in the east and north, an area that became known as the Danelaw.

q: When Elizabeth I died, the throne passed to James VI of Scotland, who became known in England as whom?
e: James VI of Scotland became James I of England, uniting the two crowns under one monarch.

q: The British Empire at its height was described as what?
o: The largest empire the world had ever seen
e: The British Empire became the largest empire the world has ever seen, covering much of the globe.

q: The German air raids on British cities during the Second World War are known as what?
e: The Blitz was the sustained German bombing of London and other cities during the war.

q: When the Spanish Armada attacked in 1588, who was the monarch of England?
e: Elizabeth I was queen when the English navy defeated the Spanish Armada.

q: The Suffragettes used which tactic to campaign for the vote?
e: The suffragettes used demonstrations and civil disobedience, and some were imprisoned.

q: Which disease returning in waves shaped life in medieval England after 1348?
e: The plague, or Black Death, returned several times after its first devastating arrival in 1348.

q: Which Catholic queen fled to England, was imprisoned, and was eventually executed on the orders of Elizabeth I?
e: Mary, Queen of Scots, a Catholic, was held prisoner for many years and executed in 1587.

q: The Hovercraft was invented by which British engineer?
e: Sir Christopher Cockerell, a British inventor, developed the hovercraft in the 1950s.

q: The Grand National horse race is run at which course?
e: The Grand National is a famous steeplechase run at Aintree, near Liverpool.

q: The Laurence Olivier Awards celebrate excellence in which field?
e: The Laurence Olivier Awards, named after the famous actor, celebrate London theatre.

q: Which famous rock formation of columns is found on the coast of Northern Ireland?
e: The Giant's Causeway is a World Heritage Site of distinctive rock columns in Northern Ireland.

q: Which annual running event takes place in the capital each spring?
e: The London Marathon is a mass-participation race held in London each year.

q: Which novelist, who used the pen name 'George Eliot', was actually a woman named Mary Ann Evans?
e: Mary Ann Evans wrote under the name George Eliot; 'Middlemarch' is among her best-known novels.

q: Which London landmark is a large Ferris wheel on the South Bank of the Thames?
e: The London Eye is a giant observation wheel beside the River Thames.

q: The British constitution is described as 'unwritten' because what?
o: It is not contained in a single written document
It was burned in a fire
e: Unlike many countries, the UK does not have a single written constitution; it is made up of laws, conventions and documents.

q: The monarch has an important ceremonial role, including opening each new session of what?
e: The monarch opens a new session of Parliament each year and reads out the government's programme.

q: The UK is one of the five permanent members of the Security Council of which body?
e: The UK is a permanent member of the UN Security Council.

q: People who are not happy with a government decision can do which of these lawfully?
o: Sign a petition or join a lawful protest
e: Citizens can campaign lawfully, for example by signing petitions, writing to MPs or joining peaceful protests.

q: Discrimination at work because of someone's religion or race is what?
e: Discrimination because of protected characteristics, including race and religion, is against the law.

q: Which of these is a way to take part in your child's education?
o: Becoming a school governor or helping at the school
Teaching only at home by law
e: Parents can get involved by becoming school governors, helping out or attending parents' events.

q: If you witness a crime, what is a responsible thing to do?
e: Reporting crime to the police helps keep the community safe; you can use 999 in an emergency or 101 otherwise.

q: Which sea separates Great Britain from Ireland?
e: The Irish Sea lies between Great Britain and the island of Ireland.

q: What are the two parts of the citizenship pledge made at a ceremony?
o: An oath/affirmation of allegiance and a pledge to respect UK rights, freedoms and laws
A tax promise and a work promise
A military oath and a trade oath
A religious vow and a cash payment
e: At the ceremony new citizens make an oath or affirmation of allegiance and a pledge to respect the UK's rights, freedoms and laws.

q: In 1066 which Norman leader became King of England?
e: William, Duke of Normandy (William the Conqueror), defeated Harold at Hastings and became King of England.

q: The attempt to blow up the Houses of Parliament in 1605 is known as what?
e: The Gunpowder Plot of 1605, involving Guy Fawkes, aimed to kill the Protestant king James I; it is remembered on Bonfire Night.

q: The slave trade was finally made illegal across the British Empire by which Act?
e: The Emancipation Act of 1833 abolished slavery throughout the British Empire; the trade itself had been banned in 1807.

q: Which British scientist's team at Bletchley Park helped break German codes in the Second World War?
e: Alan Turing led work on code-breaking and is also seen as a father of modern computing.

q: Sir Walter Raleigh is associated with introducing which crops to England from the Americas?
e: Explorers in Elizabeth I's reign, such as Raleigh, are linked with bringing tobacco and potatoes to England.

q: The partition of Ireland in 1921 created Northern Ireland, which remained part of what?
e: Northern Ireland stayed within the UK when the rest of Ireland became the Irish Free State.

q: The printing of books in English helped to do what?
o: Spread ideas and standardise the language
e: Printing, introduced by Caxton, helped spread ideas and standardise written English.

q: In which year did Ireland become formally joined with Great Britain to form the United Kingdom?
e: The Act of Union of 1801 joined Ireland with Great Britain, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.

q: Isambard Kingdom Brunel was famous as a what?
o: Engineer who built bridges, tunnels and railways
e: Brunel was one of the greatest engineers, building the Great Western Railway, bridges, tunnels and ships.

q: Which playwright, born in Stratford-upon-Avon, wrote 'Hamlet' and 'Macbeth'?
e: William Shakespeare was a playwright and poet, born in Stratford-upon-Avon.

q: Which annual film awards are run by the British Academy of Film and Television Arts?
e: The BAFTAs are the British film and television awards.

q: Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in the UK, is located in which country?
e: Ben Nevis in the Scottish Highlands is the highest mountain in the United Kingdom.

q: The home of cricket in England is often said to be which London ground?
e: Lord's Cricket Ground in London is often called the 'home of cricket'.

q: Robert Louis Stevenson, author of 'Treasure Island', came from which country?
e: Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish writer famous for 'Treasure Island' and 'Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde'.

q: Caernarfon Castle and Conwy Castle are famous medieval castles in which country?
e: These great castles in Wales were built in the reign of Edward I.

q: Which part of Parliament is made up of elected members?
e: Members of the House of Commons (MPs) are elected by the public.

q: The 'rule of law' means that what?
o: The monarch is above the law
Everyone, including those in power, must obey the law
Only citizens must obey the law
e: The rule of law means no one is above the law, including people in government.

q: The Commonwealth is an association of countries most of which were once part of what?
e: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association, most of whose members were once part of the British Empire.

q: What is the purpose of a general election?
o: To elect MPs to the House of Commons
e: A general election is held to elect MPs to represent constituencies in the House of Commons.

q: The National Health Service (NHS) provides healthcare that is mostly what?
o: Free at the point of use
Paid for in full each visit
e: The NHS provides healthcare that is mostly free at the point of use, funded through taxation.

q: What should you do with household waste to help the environment?
o: Separate and recycle it where possible
e: Recycling and reducing waste are important ways to look after the environment.

q: What does it mean that the UK is a 'constitutional monarchy'?
o: The monarch is head of state but governs within limits set by law and Parliament
e: In a constitutional monarchy the monarch is head of state but real political power lies with Parliament and ministers.

q: Which stretch of water separates England from France?
e: The English Channel separates the south of England from France.

q: Which of these is a shared value that helps people live together peacefully?
o: Tolerance of different faiths and beliefs
e: Tolerance of different faiths and beliefs is a fundamental principle of life in the UK.

q: The Battle of Hastings in 1066 is famously depicted in what?
e: The Bayeux Tapestry, which can still be seen in France, shows the events of the Norman Conquest.

q: Who commissioned the King James Bible, an English translation still used today?
e: James I ordered a new English translation of the Bible, known as the King James Version or Authorised Version.

q: The Quakers and others set up the first formal anti-slavery groups. Which man led the campaign in Parliament?
e: William Wilberforce was a leading campaigner in Parliament against the slave trade.

q: After 1945, the government led by Clement Attlee created what?
o: The National Health Service and the welfare state
e: The post-war Labour government set up the NHS in 1948 and expanded the welfare state.

q: King James I and VI was king of both England and which other country?
e: James was already King James VI of Scotland before becoming James I of England in 1603.

q: Which event in 1926 saw workers across many industries stop work in protest?
e: The General Strike of 1926 involved workers in key industries stopping work.

q: Who became the first Protestant ruler to firmly establish the Church of England after religious upheaval?
e: Elizabeth I firmly re-established the Protestant Church of England after her sister Mary's Catholic reign.

q: Which doctor developed vaccination, pioneering a vaccine against smallpox?
e: Edward Jenner developed the technique of vaccination, using it against smallpox.

q: The radar used to detect aircraft was developed by a team led by which Scottish scientist?
e: Sir Robert Watson-Watt pioneered the radar technology vital in the Second World War.

q: The famous line 'To be or not to be' comes from which Shakespeare play?
e: 'To be or not to be' is from Shakespeare's play 'Hamlet'.

q: Christmas Day is celebrated on which date?
e: Christmas Day, 25 December, celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ and is a public holiday.

q: The Tower of London, famous for the Crown Jewels, is guarded by whom?
e: The Yeoman Warders, nicknamed Beefeaters, guard the Tower of London.

q: Rugby union's home stadium in England is at which location?
e: Twickenham in London is the home of English rugby union.

q: The poet Rudyard Kipling wrote which famous poem beginning 'If'?
e: Rudyard Kipling's poem 'If' is one of the best-loved poems in Britain.

q: The White Cliffs are a famous coastal landmark near which English town?
e: The White Cliffs of Dover are a well-known landmark on the south coast of England.

q: Members of the House of Lords are generally what?
o: Not elected, including life peers and bishops
e: Members of the Lords are not elected; they include life peers, senior bishops and some hereditary peers.

q: The legal system in which part of the UK is notably different from the rest?
e: Scotland has its own distinct legal system, separate from that of England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

q: Who is the ceremonial head of the Commonwealth?
e: The monarch is the head of the Commonwealth, which has no power over its members.

q: Judges in the UK are expected to be what?
e: The judiciary is independent of government, ensuring the law is applied fairly.

q: To register with a doctor, you usually sign up with a local what?
e: People usually register with a local GP surgery for everyday health needs.

q: Paying your taxes helps to fund which of these?
o: Public services such as the NHS, schools and roads
e: Taxes pay for public services including health, education, transport and defence.

q: Which body is responsible for day-to-day running of the country?
o: The government, led by the Prime Minister
e: The government, headed by the Prime Minister and the Cabinet, runs the country day to day.

q: What is the island group that includes Great Britain and Ireland sometimes called?
e: The term 'British Isles' refers to the group of islands including Great Britain and Ireland.

q: Which of these is a public holiday in the UK, when many people do not work?
e: Bank holidays are public holidays, such as those at Christmas, Easter and in spring and summer, when many businesses close.

q: What language did the Norman ruling class speak after 1066?
e: The Norman kings and nobles spoke Norman French, which influenced the development of the English language.

q: The English Civil War was a conflict between the king and whom?
e: The Civil War was fought between the supporters of King Charles I and the supporters of Parliament.

q: After slavery was abolished, workers from which region were brought to colonies as indentured labourers?
o: India and other parts of the empire
e: Many people from India and elsewhere in the empire worked as indentured labourers after abolition.

q: Who led the team that created the National Health Service as Minister of Health?
e: Aneurin Bevan, as Minister of Health, led the establishment of the NHS in 1948.

q: The ship the 'Mayflower' carried Puritans in 1620 to settle where?
e: The Pilgrim Fathers sailed on the Mayflower to settle in America.

q: Who was the British Prime Minister who followed a policy of 'appeasement' before the Second World War?
e: Neville Chamberlain pursued appeasement towards Nazi Germany before the war.

q: The 'Golden Age' of exploration and the arts in England took place under which monarch?
e: Elizabeth I's reign is often called a golden age, with writers like Shakespeare and explorers like Drake.

q: The 'Spinning Jenny', which improved cloth-making, was invented by whom?
e: James Hargreaves invented the Spinning Jenny, an important machine in the textile industry.

q: Which British physicist split the atom in 1917 and is called the father of nuclear physics?
e: Ernest Rutherford was the first person to split the atom.

q: Which Scottish poet wrote in the Scots language and is celebrated on Burns Night?
e: Robert Burns, known as 'the Bard', wrote poems and songs in Scots; Burns Night is held on 25 January.

q: What is traditionally eaten as a main Christmas meal in the UK?
e: Roast turkey with vegetables is a traditional Christmas meal, often followed by Christmas pudding.

q: Which building in Edinburgh is a famous castle dominating the city skyline?
e: Edinburgh Castle is a well-known landmark in the Scottish capital.

q: Darts, snooker and football are examples of what?
e: These are among the sports widely followed and played in the UK.

q: Which comic actor and filmmaker from London became a global star of silent films?
e: Charlie Chaplin, born in London, became famous worldwide for his silent films.

q: The Giant's Causeway and the Titanic Quarter are attractions in which city/region?
e: The Giant's Causeway is in Northern Ireland, and the Titanic (built in Belfast) is remembered in the Titanic Quarter.

q: The area represented by one MP is called what?
e: A constituency is the area that each MP is elected to represent.

q: Criminal law deals with what?
o: Behaviour the state has made illegal, such as theft and violence
e: Criminal law covers crimes that the state punishes, such as theft, assault and drug offences.

q: What should you do if you want to stand for public office, such as becoming a councillor?
o: You can stand for election if you are eligible
You must be appointed by the monarch
e: Citizens who meet the requirements can stand for election to local councils and other public offices.

q: If you are arrested, which of these rights do you have?
o: To be treated fairly and, in serious cases, to have legal representation
To be tried without a court
e: People who are arrested have legal rights, including fair treatment and, where appropriate, access to legal advice.

q: If you need urgent medical help but it is not life-threatening, you can call which number?
e: NHS 111 provides advice for urgent but non-emergency health problems; 999 is for emergencies.

q: The money you pay for a television licence helps fund what?
e: The TV licence fee funds the BBC's services.

q: A citizen who disagrees with a new law can lawfully do which of these?
o: Campaign and lobby their MP to change it
e: People can campaign peacefully, write to their MP and join groups to try to change laws they disagree with.

q: Which of these is the largest country within the UK by area and population?
e: England is the largest of the four countries of the UK by both area and population.

q: Learning about the UK's history and traditions helps a new resident to do what?
o: Take a fuller part in the life of their community
e: Understanding the UK's history and traditions helps people integrate and take part in community life.

q: The Domesday Book was compiled on the orders of which king?
e: William the Conqueror ordered the Domesday Book, a survey of England's land and people, completed in 1086.

q: Supporters of Parliament in the Civil War were nicknamed what?
e: Parliament's supporters were called Roundheads, while the king's supporters were called Cavaliers.

q: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 for how long, the longest of any monarch up to that time?
e: Victoria reigned for almost 64 years, longer than any previous monarch, a period called the Victorian Age.

q: The 1950s saw people invited from which region to help rebuild Britain after the war?
o: The West Indies, India and Pakistan
e: Workers from the West Indies, India, Pakistan and elsewhere were invited to help fill labour shortages.

q: Which disease spread rapidly in the crowded city of London in 1665?
e: The Great Plague of 1665 killed a large number of people in London.

q: The 'Battle of Britain' in 1940 was fought mainly where?
e: The Battle of Britain was an air battle in which the RAF defeated the German Luftwaffe.

q: The settlement of Protestants in Ulster during the reign of James I is known as what?
e: The Plantation of Ulster saw Protestant settlers from England and Scotland given land in the north of Ireland.

q: Canals were built across Britain during the Industrial Revolution mainly to do what?
e: A network of canals was built to move goods and raw materials for the growing industries.

q: The first cash dispenser (ATM) and other inventions reflect the UK's strength in what field?
e: The UK has a long history of scientific and technological innovation.

q: The Romantic poets included Wordsworth, Byron, Shelley and which other?
e: William Blake was among the Romantic poets, along with Wordsworth, Byron, Shelley and Keats.

q: New Year is celebrated on 1 January, but the Scottish celebration is especially known and called what?
e: Hogmanay is the Scottish celebration of New Year, sometimes a bigger event than Christmas there.

q: The National Trust was founded to do what?
o: Preserve important buildings, coastline and countryside
e: The National Trust works to preserve places of historic interest and natural beauty.

q: The National Lottery, launched in 1994, gives much of its money to what?
o: Good causes such as sport, arts and heritage
e: The National Lottery raises money for good causes including the arts, sport, heritage and charities.

q: The film director Alfred Hitchcock was famous for making which kind of films?
e: Alfred Hitchcock, a British director, was known as the 'master of suspense'.

q: The famous luxury ocean liner Titanic was built in which city?
e: The Titanic was built in Belfast, Northern Ireland.

q: How is the Prime Minister normally determined?
o: The leader of the party that wins the most seats in the Commons
Appointed by the House of Lords
e: The Prime Minister is usually the leader of the party that wins a majority of seats in the House of Commons.

q: Civil law deals with what kind of matters?
o: Disputes between people or organisations, such as debt or housing
e: Civil law covers disputes between individuals or groups, for example over money, housing or employment.

q: Freedom of speech in the UK means people can do what?
o: Say anything with no limits at all
Express opinions, within the limits of the law
e: People are free to express their views, as long as they stay within the law and do not incite hatred or violence.

q: Solicitors and barristers are types of what?
e: Solicitors and barristers are legal professionals who advise and represent people in legal matters.

q: To report a crime that is not an emergency, which number can you call?
e: You can call 101 to contact the police about a non-emergency.

q: Which of these is a role a citizen can take on in the justice system?
e: Serving on a jury is one way citizens take part in the justice system.

q: Who makes sure that government departments spend public money properly?
e: Parliament holds the government to account, including over how it spends public money.

q: The Severn and the Thames are examples of what in the UK?
e: The River Severn and the River Thames are among the UK's major rivers.

q: The UK is a diverse society made up of people of many what?
o: Different ethnic origins, cultures and religions
e: The UK is a diverse society with people of many different backgrounds, cultures and faiths.
